Preface

This book is the result of a long‐standing collaboration among the three authors, which began when Carla Moreira was a PhD student under the supervision of Jacobo de Uña‐Álvarez. Carla successfully defended her thesis, entitled ‘The Statistical Analysis of Doubly Truncated Data: New Methods, Software Development, and Biomedical Applications’, at the Universidade de Vigo in July 2010. At that time, only a small number of people seemed to be aware of the importance of random double truncation. Research papers on this topic were scarce before 2010, with the contribution by Bradley Efron and Vahe Petrosian in 1999 as the most relevant one. And, of course, no software was available. So, for us, it was a risky and exciting research exercise to embrace such an initiative.

We launched version 1.1 of our R package DTDA in September 2009. To our knowledge this was the first software library implementing the Efron–Petrosian estimator. The package included Efron and Petrosian's data on quasar luminosities, and we are very thankful to both scientists for sharing them. DTDA has been downloaded more than 45 thousand times up to now. We have taken the opportunity of writing this book to update and enhance DTDA, feeding it with new illustrative real datasets and enabling new functions and capabilities. We are confident in that the update of the package and the guidance provided by this book will exponentially increase the applications involving doubly truncated data, and also raise awareness about the implications of double truncation on inferential procedures.

Over these years, several researchers have collaborated with us in the fascinating adventure of investigating double truncation. Among them, we would like to mention Ingrid Van Keilegom, Micha Mandel, Rebecca Betensky, Luis Meira‐Machado and Roel Braekers. We have enjoyed co‐authoring a number of research papers with them. We also learned a lot about double truncation by studying real data problems posed by applied researchers; here we thank María José Bento, David Keith Simon, Zhi‐Sheng Ye, Ana Cristina Santos and Henrique Barros for fruitful discussions and cooperation.

Nowadays, there is a considerable statistical community doing research on exploratory and inferential methods for doubly truncated data, partly motivated by new emerging applications in Biomedicine, Economics and Engineering, among other fields. At the time of writing the activity in this area of research is much more intense than ever before, as is evident from the number of papers on the topic published in the last couple of years. And the interest in double truncation is growing faster and faster!

This book aims to serve as a companion for those ones interested in learning about doubly truncated data analysis and inference, presenting a wide range of tools for estimating distribution and regression models. All the methods presented in this book are accompanied by real data and simulated examples and, at the end of each chapter, the reader will find the do‐it‐yourself code, mostly based on the DTDA package. This book is not written with the aim of being just read: its main purpose is to invite the reader to think, explore and experience.

This volume is also self‐contained, providing a general overview on the main results. Further technical details and some omitted proofs can be consulted in the original references. It is also in our intention to leave several take‐home messages. First, that the correction of the potential sampling bias arising from double truncation may be critical in estimation and inference. Second, that, even when the Efron–Petrosian estimator is conceptually complicated and its asymptotic theory may be overwhelming, its practical application is relatively simple from the available software packages and the good performance of resampling algorithms. Third, that external information on the sampling bias should be used whenever available, since the Efron–Petrosian estimator may be very noisy or even non‐existing, particularly when the sample size is small to moderate.

We frankly hope that the reader will enjoy (and experience!) the book, at least as much as we have enjoyed writing it! Comments and suggestions from the readers on this edition are welcome; please send them to jacobo@uvigo.es to help us to improve the book.

Parts of this book were written while the authors were supported by the Grants MTM2017‐89422‐P (MINECO/AEI/FEDER, UE) (first author), UIDB/00013/2020 and UIDP/00013/2020 (second author), and MTM2016‐76969‐P (MINECO/AEI/FEDER, UE) (third author). This is acknowledged.

Introduction

1.1 Random Truncation

Random truncation generally refers to a situation in which a number of individuals of the target population cannot be sampled because a certain random event precludes them. When this random event is unrelated to the variables of interest standard statistical methods apply, with the only inconvenience of using a smaller sample size. In many practical cases, however, the truncation event is related to the variables under study, and specific methods to overcome the sampling bias must be considered.

This book is focused on random truncation phenomena that arise (usually, but not only) when sampling time‐to‐event data. That is, the variable of interest is the time elapsed from a well‐defined origin to another well‐defined end point. In this setting, a truncated sample of is a set of independent and identically distributed (iid) random variables with the conditional distribution of given , where is a random set. Since the truncation event is obviously related to , standard statistical methods applied to the truncated sample may be systematically biased. For example, the ordinary empirical cumulative distribution function (ecdf) of at point , , converges to rather than to the target cumulative distribution function (cdf) . This problem has received remarkable attention since the seminal paper by Turnbull (1976). Special forms of truncation when sampling time‐to‐event data are reviewed in Sections 1.2 and 1.3.

Time‐to‐event data are relevant in fields like Survival Analysis and Reliability Engineering, in which random truncation often occurs. Random truncation is found in Astronomy too, where represents the luminosity of an stellar object that is subject to observation limits. Examples from these areas will be introduced and analysed throughout this book.

1.2 One‐sided Truncation

1.2.1 Left‐truncation

Left‐truncation is a common feature when sampling time‐to‐event data. A left‐truncation time for the target is defined as a random variable such that is observed only when , determining the random set in the previous section.

Left‐truncation occurs, for example, with cross‐sectional sampling, where the sampled individuals are those being between the origin and the end point at a certain calendar time, which is the cross‐section date (Wang, 1991). That is, the observer arrives at the process at a given date, being allowed to observe the time‐to‐event and the left‐truncation time for the individuals 'in progress' by that date. With cross‐sectional sampling, the variable is simply defined as the time from onset to the cross‐section date. This sampling procedure is often applied because it entails relatively little effort to reach a pre‐specified sampling size. In medical research, such a design leads to the sampling of the so‐called prevalent cases: patients already diagnosed from a certain disease of interest who survived beyond the cross‐section date. Clearly, such a sampling design implies an observational bias, in the sense that individuals with longer survival (the value) will be observed with a relatively large probability. There exist well investigated proposals to overcome such a bias, based on the simple idea of taking the observed left‐truncation times into account to define suitable risk sets. For this purpose, independence between and has been traditionally assumed. This independence assumption states that the time‐to‐event distribution remains unchanged along time, being unrelated to the date of onset. A classical example of left‐truncation are the Channing House data, where the age at death is measured for people living in that retirement centre; in this case, the target variable is left‐truncated by the age when entering the residence (Klein and Moeschberger, 2003).

Another feature leading to left‐truncation is the delayed entry into study. This happens when the individuals enter the study only at some random time after onset. For example, diagnosis of a certain disease may not be ascertained until the first visit to the hospital. If the 'end‐of‐disease' event occurs before the potential date of visit, the time‐to‐event of such a patient will be never known, with the resulting difficulty in observing relatively small event times. Beyersmann et al. (2012) provide an illustrative example of this issue in the investigation of abortion times.

1.2.2 Right‐truncation

In some particular settings, the target variable of ultimate interest is observed only for the individuals who experience the event before a certain calendar time . A typical example of such a situation is the investigation of the incubation (or induction) times for AIDS; see for example Klein and Moeschberger (2003). The incubation time is defined as the time elapsed between the date of HIV infection, say, and the development of AIDS. If stands for the incubation time and , then the incubation times of individuals developing AIDS prior follow the distribution of conditionally on . Here, is called the right‐truncation time. An immediate effect of right‐truncation is that large values of are sampled with a relatively small probability.

1.2.3 Truncation vs. Censoring

At this point, the reader may be curious about the difference between truncation and censoring. Right‐censoring is a very well known phenomenon in Survival Analysis and reliability studies, among other fields. It happens when the follow‐up of a given individual stops before the event of interest has taken place. In such a case, the observer only knows that the target variable is larger than the registered value, which is referred to as censoring time. A sample made up of real and censored values is typically analysed by the Kaplan–Meier estimator (Kaplan and Meier, 1958), which corrects for the fact that some of the recorded values for are smaller than the true ones. With truncated data, every value in the sample corresponds to a true observation of ; however, the distribution of the observed values may be shifted with respect to the true one due to the truncation event. This difference between truncation and censoring suggests that specific methods to estimate the target distribution under random truncation should be employed. Indeed, Woodroofe (1985) provides a deep analysis of one‐sided truncation, introducing the original idea of Lynden–Bell (1971) as a nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) of the probability distribution in that setting. The estimator in Woodroofe (1985) is a particular case of the estimator corresponding to doubly truncated data, on which this book is focused.

1.3 Double Truncation

A variable of interest is said to be doubly truncated by a couple of random variables if the observation of is possible only when occurs. In such a case, and are called left‐ and right‐truncation variables respectively. Double truncation reduces to left‐truncation when degenerates at , while it corresponds to right‐truncation when . This book is focused on the problem of estimating the distribution of , and other related curves, from a set of iid triplets with the distribution of given .

There are several scenarios where double truncation appears in practice. One setting leading to double truncation is that of interval sampling, where the sample is restricted to the individuals with event between two specific dates and (Zhu and Wang, 2012). Then, the right‐truncation time is , where denotes the date of onset for the time‐to‐event, and the left‐truncation time is , where is the interval width. The Childhood Cancer Data in Section 1.4.1 is an example of data obtained through interval sampling.

With interval sampling the variable is degenerated at . This occurs in other sampling schemes too, in which and are certain subject‐specific event dates. An illustrative example is given by the Parkinson's Disease Data, see Section 1.4.5, where is the individual age at blood sampling. When is constant, the couple falls on a line, and its joint density does not exist, even when the truncating variables may be continuous.

In other situations, the truncating variables and are not linked through the linear equation . For example, and could represent some random observation limits beyond which the variable of interest can not be sampled or detected. Situations like this occur for example in Astronomy, as it is illustrated in Section 1.4.4.

With random double truncation, both large and small values of are observed in principle with a relatively small probability. However, the real observational bias for varies from application to application, depending on the joint distribution of . We will see, for example, that the probability of sampling a value , namely , may be roughly constant, inducing no observational bias; or that it may be roughly decreasing, indicating the dominance of the right‐truncation bias relative to the left‐truncation bias.

Another issue of relevance is that of the identifiability of the distribution of . Intuitively it is clear that with doubly truncated data it is only possible to estimate the distribution of conditional on , where and denote respectively the lower and upper endpoints of the supports of and (see Chapter 2 for details). This may have important practical consequences, as we will see. On the other hand, in applications with doubly truncated survival data the estimates correspond to the susceptible population for which the terminal event of interest is sure. This is in contrast to the standard analysis of survival times where a portion of the individuals may belong to the so‐called cured fraction, or immunes. This should be taken into account when interpreting the results from the analysis.

An important difference of double truncation when compared to one‐sided truncation is that, with doubly truncated data, the NPMLE of the probability distribution has no explicit form. In fact, the NPMLE may be non‐unique and even non‐existing (Xiao and Hudgens, 2019); see Chapter 2. Several iterative algorithms that have been proposed to compute the NPMLE in practice (Efron and Petrosian, 1999; Shen, 2010) will be reviewed in this book, and simulated and real data examples will be analysed with existing libraries of the software R. Semiparametric and parametric alternatives to the NPMLE will be introduced too; these approaches avoid some of the aforementioned potential issues of non‐uniqueness or non‐existence of the NPMLE, also reducing the variance at the price of introducing some bias in estimation. Also, resampling procedures, testing problems, smoothing methods, regression models and multi‐state data analysis under double truncation will be presented.

1.4 Real Data Examples

In this section we introduce the datasets that will be used throughout the book for illustration purposes. All of them suffer from double truncation. These examples are available within the last update of the DTDA package (Moreira et al., 2021a).

1.4.1 Childhood Cancer Data

The Childhood Cancer Data were gathered from the IPO (Instituto Português de Oncologia) of Porto, Portugal, by the RORENO (Registro Oncológico do Norte) service. The information corresponds to all children diagnosed from cancer between 1 January 1999 () and 31 December 2003 () in the region of North Portugal, which includes five districts: Porto, Braga, Bragança, Vila Real and Viana do Castelo. The variable of main interest is the age at diagnosis which, by definition of childhood cancer, is supported on the interval (time in years). The number of cases was 409. However, for three cases the value of was not available, so we only consider the children who report complete information.

Because of the interval sampling, the age at diagnosis is doubly truncated by the pair , where the right‐truncation variable is the time in years from birth (date of onset, ) to 31 December 2003, and . The triplets , , with the values observed for were reported in Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez (2010), while de Uña‐Álvarez (2020) included the cancer group in the statistical analysis. Ordinary descriptive statistics can be applied to the information gathered along this 5 year long window to compute, for instance, the average age at cancer diagnosis. However, if the goal is to describe the population of children eventually developing cancer, the double truncation issue should be acknowledged and properly corrected, so potential biases are avoided.

Interestingly, the observed values for range between and 14.5 (years); equivalently, the observed values for range between 0.5 and 19.5. This means that the lower and upper endpoints of and satisfy and . Thus, in this case, the target variable is observable on its whole support , and there are no identification issues for , the cdf of . Information on is summarized in Table 1.1.

This dataset is used in Chapters 2, 3 and 5 and is accessible in the DTDA package in ChildCancer.

1.4.2 AIDS Blood Transfusion Data

Kalbfleish and Lawless (1989) reported 494 cases of transfusion‐related AIDS, corresponding to individuals diagnosed prior to 1 July 1986 (). The variable of ultimate interest is the induction or incubation time, which is the time elapsed from HIV infection to AIDS. Importantly, HIV was unknown before 1982 (); this implies that cases developing AIDS prior to this date were not reported. Let denote the time from HIV infection to 1 July 1986 (in months), and introduce ; then, due to the interval sampling, only triplets satisfying were observed (Bilker and Wang, 1996). We restrict our analysis to the cases with consistent data, for which the infection could be attributed to a single transfusion or a short series of transfusions. This dataset is fully reported in Kalbfleish and Lawless (1989), p. 361.

The observed values of range from 0.5 to 89 (months), while ranges from to 45.5. This suggests that the lower limit of the support of is about , while the upper limit of the support of is about 99.5. As discussed in Chapter 2, in such a case the distribution of the incubation time is identifiable on the interval (months). The AIDS Blood Transfusion Data also includes information on the age of the individual at infection; see Table 1.2.

This dataset is used in Chapters 2, 3, 4 and 5 and can be obtained from AIDS.DT in DTDA package.

1.4.3 Equipment‐ S Rounded Failure Time Data

Companies are often interested in estimating the time to failure of their devices after installation. For doing this, maintenance departments may register events of failure between two specific dates and for the units installed in the field. This field lifetime distribution is, however, doubly truncated because of the interval sampling. The Equipment‐ S data (Ye and Tang, 2016) concern failures of a certain device (details are not given due to confidentiality issues) recorded between 1996 and 2011, a 15 year long observational window. Information on the date of installation and the date of failure, rounded to years, was obtained by digitizing Figure 2 in the referred paper. This dataset is therefore a discrete version of the original data in Ye and Tang (2016). In this example the right‐truncation time is the number of years between installation and 2011, while the left‐truncation time is just . In Table 1.3 the Equipment‐ S failure times are summarized.

The observable range for the Equipment‐ S failure times goes from zero to 34 years, which is the maximum observed value for the right‐truncating variable ; hence, estimation of the reliability can only be done conditional on failure within the first 34 years of operation.

EqSRounded in the DTDA package contains this dataset, which is used in Chapter 2.

1.4.4 Quasar Data

A classical motivating example of doubly truncated data, introduced by Efron and Petrosian (1999), is found in cosmology when registering the luminosity of quasars. Quasars are observed only if the luminosity lies within a certain interval, bounded at both ends that are determined by detection limits of observation devices, so the data suffer from double truncation. The original dataset studied by Efron and Petrosian (1999) comprises triplets , where is the luminosity in the log‐scale, obtained from a transformation model based on the redshift and the apparent magnitude of the th quasar. See Efron and Petrosian (1999) for further details on the transformation model. Due to experimental constraints, the distribution of each luminosity in the log‐scale is truncated to a known interval . Specifically, quasars with apparent magnitude above were too dim to yield dependent redshifts, and hence they were excluded from the study. In addition, the lower limit was used to avoid confusion with non‐quasar stellar objects. Some descriptive statistics are provided in Table 1.4.

The Quasar Data are used in Chapter 3. This classical example is also included in the DTDA package (dataset Quasars).

1.4.5 Parkinson's Disease Data

Clark et al. (2011) investigated the association of candidate single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and age of onset of Parkinson's disease (PD). For this, genomic DNA samples from human blood samples were obtained from the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) Human Genetics DNA and Cell Line Repository at the Coriell Institute for Medical Research (Camden, New Jersey). More specifically, one aim of the study was to detect association between the rs8192678 PGC‐1a and A10398G SNPs and the risk or age of onset of PD.

In order to remove the selection bias related to survival, the study was limited to patients diagnosed from PD who had their DNA sample taken within 8 years after onset. Consequently, the age of onset is right truncated by the age at blood sampling , and it is left truncated by (age in years). Clark et al. (2011) considered only the right‐truncation issue, but ignored left‐truncation. Both truncation limits were taken into account however in several re‐analyses of the PD data, including Austin et al. (2014) and Mandel et al. (2018).

Clark et al. (2011) divided the cases into an earlier age of onset group (35–55 years) with 99 patients, and a later age of onset group (63–87 years) with 100 patients. The genetic information of these cases, together with basic statistics on the age of onset, is reported in Table 1.5. The early onset group have two patients with missing data on A10398G SNP and on age at sampling, and these are excluded from the analysis.

The Parkinson's Disease Data are used in Chapters 2 and 4. Access to this dataset is possible through the DTDA package, which includes the data frames PDearly and PDlate, for the early and late onset groups, respectively.

1.4.6 Acute Coronary Syndrome Data

We also consider data on the age at diagnosis of acute coronary syndrome (ACS). In Portugal, with a population of 10.3 million inhabitants, there are 38 public hospitals with resources for structured care of patients with ACS, out of which 16 have catheterization laboratory facilities. Public hospitals provide treatment for the majority of the acute coronary events and the number of patients submitted to primary percutaneous coronary intervention increased by 37.0% from 2009 to 2013, although at the regional level access to this procedure varied. The EPIHeart study (Araújo et al., 2018) is a study assembled between August 2013 and December 2014 by the Cardiology Department of two tertiary hospitals in two regions in Northern Portugal: Hospital de São João, Porto, covering the metropolitan area of Porto in the coast; and Hospital de São Pedro, Vila Real, covering the interior, northeastern region. The inclusion criteria to the cohort were admission with confirmed diagnosis of type 1 (primary spontaneous) ACS, aged 18 years or older, and living in the catchment area of the referred hospitals (Porto, Vila Real, Bragança or Viseu). Data were collected through structured interviews within the first 48 hours after admission. Of the 1297 patients initially considered, 939 were included in the cohort due the inclusion criteria (Moreira et al., 2021b). Some descriptive statistics can be found in Table 1.6.

The age at diagnosis , ranging from 29.42 to 94.09 years old, was doubly truncated by (), where stands for the elapsed time (in years) between birth and end of the study (December 2014), and .

The ACS Data are used in Chapters 2 and 3. This dataset can be obtained from ACS (complete dataset) or ACSred (reduced dataset) in the DTDA package.

2
One‐Sample Problems

The problem of estimating a cdf from a random sample of individuals taken from a homogeneous population is addressed in this chapter. Under double truncation the sampling information includes the variable of interest and the left‐truncation and right‐truncation variables and , but the observable population reduces to those individuals for which . Therefore, we assume that the data at hand , , are a random sample following the conditional distribution of given . Of course, will be satisfied for .

We consider the sample size as a non‐random quantity. Under an alternative viewpoint, the data result from a two‐step procedure. In the first step, a random sample of with size , , , is obtained from the target population. In the second step, the triplets violating the condition are discarded. This entails that the size of the final sample is indeed random (see Woodroofe (1985) for further discussions). We will proceed conditionally on , which is the standard approach, ignoring the additional binomial term that would arise from the randomness of .

The focus is the estimation of along the support of the variable. In Section 2.1 this problem is addressed under a nonparametric viewpoint, while in Section 2.2 alternative estimators based on semiparametric and parametric models are considered.

2.1 Nonparametric Estimation of a Distribution Function

A naive estimator of is the ordinary ecdf of the 's, given by

(2.1)

However, as discussed in Chapter 1, this estimator may be systematically biased. In general, the limit of as is , which may not be equal to the target . The possible bias of as an estimator of is nicely illustrated through the weighting function, or biasing function, which reports, for each value of the variable, its sampling probability. This biasing function is defined for each point in the support of as

(2.2)

Note that the second equality in (2.2) holds true if and are independent random variables. Throughout the book we assume that such an independence condition is satisfied, unless otherwise is indicated.

When there is no truncation (), the biasing function is constant. This indicates that, once a particular value of the variable is drawn from the population, its chances to be included in the final sample are not affected by . Under left‐truncation (), reduces to the cdf of the left‐truncation variable, thus being monotone non‐decreasing. This non‐decreasing shape of the biasing function indicates that larger values of have relatively more chances to be observed. The situation under right‐truncation is just the opposite; in this case, is one minus the cdf of the right‐truncation variable (that is, the survival function of ). In the following section we introduce the NPMLE of in the general setting of double truncation. As mentioned, the NPMLE has no explicit form and, in practice, must be computed by iterative algorithms.

Nonparametric estimators of alternative to the NPMLE in Section 2.1.1 have been proposed in the related literature. For instance, Austin et al. (2014) proposed a nonparametric estimator under the additional assumption of independence between and . When the truncation limits are independent, (2.2) can be simply estimated by a product of two Lynden‐Bell estimators, and an explicit‐form estimator of can be constructed. Unfortunately, the assumption of independence between and is often unrealistic and, in particular, it excludes the important scenario of interval sampling. Another non‐iterative estimator of is the one proposed by de Uña‐Álvarez (2018), which estimates recursively from left to right, by using the family of Lynden‐Bell estimators computed from the restricted samples , . This nonparametric estimator is well adapted to interval sampling; however, it is not efficient. None of these alternative nonparametric procedures is covered by the current manuscript.

In the following examples we illustrate the application of this result, which is somehow related to the issue of holes in the Lynden‐Bell estimation (Strzalkowska‐Kominiak and Stute, 2010). At this point we mention that the possible non‐existence and non‐uniqueness of the NPMLE may affect simulation studies too; we have found such a situation in a small number of Monte Carlo trials drawn from the simulation scenarios introduced in Section 2.1.3 below. Obviously, the issue may appear when using resampling procedures too. It should be noted that for all datasets considered in this book, except for the ACS Data, the existence and uniqueness condition is satisfied. 2.1.2 Numerical Algorithms for Computing the NPMLE

In what follows, we review three existing algorithms for the computation of the NPMLE of the target distribution : the two algorithms proposed by Efron and Petrosian (1999) and the coupled algorithm proposed by Shen (2010a). This last proposal also provides an estimate for . The algorithms are iterative, so they start with an initial solution for and then they proceed by improving it step by step until fulfilling a certain convergence criterion.

Shen's algorithm

  1. S1. Compute the initial from the initial solution .
  2. S2. Apply Eq. (2.13) to get a first estimator of , namely , and compute the corresponding .
  3. S3. Apply Eq. (2.16) to improve , getting say, and compute the corresponding .
  4. S4. Repeat steps S2 and S3 until convergence.

Algorithm S1–S4 provides a solution for equal to that of the first Efron–Petrosian algorithm. On the other hand, the second Efron–Petrosian algorithm is based on a different set of equations and, thus, it is not obvious in principle that it will always provide the same solution for . The aforementioned Hazard Rate Theorem of Efron and Petrosian (1999) gives, however, theoretical support for the validity of L1–L3. Indeed, as already indicated by Efron and Petrosian (1999), L1–L3 is expected to result in a faster convergence when the right truncation is not severe; this is the situation of the Quasar Data of Section 1.4.4. For the Quasar Data example, EP1–EP3 (and S1–S4) required 43 iterations, while L1–L3 stopped after only 7 iterations when applied with the same, default convergence criterion of the DTDA package.

In this section we describe the theoretical properties of the NPMLE for doubly truncated data. This includes consistency results, but also a representation of the NPMLE as a sum of iid random variables that allows for an inspection of its sampling distribution. Apart from the results pertaining to itself, we provide the properties of functionals of the form

2.1.4 Standard Errors and Confidence Limits

In the previous section we have seen that the NPMLE asymptotically follows a Gaussian distribution centered at the target , with standard deviation say. This is the asymptotic standard deviation of as . In other words, for large the standard error of approximately equals . Unfortunately, there is no simple explicit formula for that may suggest a plug‐in type estimator for the standard error. Thus, alternative procedures are needed.

The bootstrap has been traditionally used for the estimation of standard errors and, more generally, sampling distributions in a variety of settings. For randomly truncated data, two different bootstrap resampling plans have been proposed and investigated: the simple bootstrap (SB), and the obvious bootstrap (OB). While the SB resamples with replacement from , the OB requires the preliminary estimation of and in order to proceed. Specifically, the OB obtains the ‐value from , the couple is independently drawn from and, finally, the triplet is discarded if or occurs. This procedure is repeated until a valid triplet satisfying is obtained. Therefore, the OB gives positive weights to triplets with , where (unlike for the SB) is possible. For clarity and ease of reference these resampling plans are detailed in the following two definitions.

Definition 2.1.20   Simple bootstrap (SB). Given the iid observations , a simple bootstrap resample is a triplet with discrete uniform distribution on ; that is, , .

Definition 2.1.21   Obvious bootstrap (OB). Given the iid observations , an obvious bootstrap resample is obtained from two discrete random variables and supported on and respectively, and such that and , . The triplet is kept conditionally on .

In the left‐truncated setting the differences between the SB and OB methods have been discussed by Gross and Lai (1996), who also investigated the theoretical validity of the simple bootstrap for left‐truncated and right‐censored data by using Edgeworth expansions. In their setting the application of the OB is not straightforward because it involves either smoothing or an independence condition between the truncating and the residual right‐censoring variables. Without censoring, however, such complications are not present, even when truncation occurs from both (left and right) sides. Theory for the bootstrap with doubly truncated data has not been developed yet.

The previous bootstrap approaches can be used for estimating the standard error of and, subsequently, for computing confidence intervals. Specifically, Emura et al. (2015) and de Uña‐Álvarez (2020) analyzed the accuracy of the standard error of based on the SB. The simulation studies in these papers indicate a good behavior of the method, also for sample sizes as small as . Therefore, even when the knowledge on the theoretical properties of the SB in the doubly truncated setting is limited and one should be cautious, we generally recommend it in applications.

In order to illustrate and compare the performance of the two bootstrap methods introduced in Definitions 2.1.20 and 2.1.21, we report some simulation results considering the scenarios I and II described in Section 2.1.3, which correspond to situations without/with sampling bias for , respectively. We focus first on the estimation of the standard error, by SB and OB, and taking as a benchmark the true standard error, approximated from a large number of Monte Carlo replicates. In Table 2.2 (scenario I) and Table 2.3 (scenario II) the average and the standard deviation of the quotients between the bootstrap standard error, , and the true one, , are given. Only results for three deciles (0.3, 0.5 and 0.7) are shown, although similar conclusions can be obtained for other quantiles. Both SB and OB methods perform well; the average of the ratio approaches 1 and the standard deviation of the ratio reduces as the the sample size increases. In Table 2.2 we also report the value of standard error of the ordinary ecdf (denoted by ), which is a consistent estimator in the scenario without sampling bias, yielding values around one‐third of . This illustrates the variance increase due to the double truncation.

Standard errors can be seen as the simplest way to gain information about the variability of a given estimator. However, often this variability is better visualized by means of confidence intervals. With doubly truncated data SB and OB methods can be used to this aim, as we will elaborate now. Other alternative routes for producing confidence intervals under double truncation include empirical likelihood ratio (Shen, 2011) and explicit formulae (Emura et al., 2015).

Although other alternatives are possible (such as the consideration of an arcsin‐square root transformation), we will consider a simple log‐transform. One of these alternative methods is the percentile bootstrap. The percentile bootstrap considers the collection of bootstrap NPMLEs and takes the corresponding and quantiles; that is, the values of the are sorted and the ones in the positions and are taken as limits of the confidence interval. The behavior of (2.23) and (2.24) is illustrated in the simulation scenarios I and II in Section 2.1.3, see Tables 2.4 and 2.5. Although other alternatives were checked (such as the normal confidence intervals or the basic bootstrap method), the best results were obtained for these two strategies. It can be seen that both the log‐transformed and the percentile confidence intervals show a very similar behavior: the empirical coverage is quite close to the nominal coverage (which was fixed to 95%), even for , with a considerable reduction in length (average length in parentheses) as the sample size increases. It should be also noticed that the log‐transformed approach, although showing satisfactory results in general, may be problematic for low quantiles and small sample sizes. In these cases, a null value of may appear and, if so, the log‐transform procedure cannot be applied. In Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez (2010a) further empirical evidence on the performance of the percentile method based on both SB and OB is provided.

The previous methods to compute confidence intervals for enable the construction of pointwise confidence bands for the cdf under double truncation. One may argue that such bands do not guarantee a global coverage of the target curve. As an alternative to bootstrap methods, Emura et al. (2015) propose a closed‐form estimator for the asymptotic covariance function of the NPMLE, enabling the construction of global (equal precision and Kolmogorov–Smirnov type) confidence bands. Through some simulation experiments using bootstrap replicates the authors observe a slightly better performance of the equal precision bands and the expected conservative behavior of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov bands, as it happens for non‐truncated data. Actually, both approaches are inspired in the confidence bands for censored data (see Klein and Moeschberger (2003), Section 4.4), originally proposed by Nair (1984) for the equal prediction bands and Hall and Wellner (1980) for the Kolmogorov‐Smirnov bands.

2.2 Semiparametric and Parametric Approaches

In particular applications with doubly truncated data, external information on the cdf of the truncating couple is available. Under interval sampling, for instance, is determined by the rate of the birth process, which may fit a specific known pattern. A prominent example is the stationary case, in which the birth process follows an homogeneous Poisson model. In such a case, both the left and right truncation limits are uniformly distributed on their corresponding support intervals, so and are fully specified linear functions. This seems to be the situation of the Childhood Cancer Data in Section 1.4.1: the NPMLE of for this dataset is depicted in Figure 2.13, left, and it is very close to the uniform distribution on the interval . Indeed, since Portuguese demographics indicate a roughly constant number of alive births over the period 1984–2003, it is reasonable to assume that the birth process for the subpopulation developing cancer before the age of 15 is driven by a constant‐rate Poisson process. Such external information, when available, can be used to improve the estimation of the target . In other applications the information on the birth process is hardly available. For example, for the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data of Section 1.4.2, is essentially the infection date, and external information on the date of transfusions involving the infected blood is missing. In this case, the NPMLE of is non‐uniform, see Figure 2.13, right, suggesting a non‐homogeneous Poisson model for the infection process. So very different situations may appear in practice.

The semiparametric setting refers to a situation in which is known to belong to a parametric family of bivariate cdfs, , where the parametric space is a subset of the euclidean space . When has a single element, one falls within the aforementioned example of a fully specified truncation distribution. More generally, will be a convex set of possible values for the ‐dimensional vector . In this setting improved estimation of is attained by means of the preliminary estimation of ; this approach is explored in Section 2.2.1. Semiparametric truncation models have been previously considered under one‐sided truncation (Wang, 1989), and also recently extended for left‐truncated and right‐censored data (Huang et al., 2015; Heuchenne et al., 2020).

An alternative semiparametric setting is that in which is assumed to follow a certain parametric model, say, while remains nonparametric. Since is the target, the scenario can be called ‘parametric’ rather than 'semiparametric'. Estimation and inference procedures for this setting is considered in Section 2.2.2.

2.2.1 Semiparametric Approach

In Section 2.1.1 the NPMLE of was represented as an IPWE, where is upweighted according to its estimated sampling probability ; see Eq. (2.7). In the semiparametric setting, where belongs to the distribution family , the sampling probability is written as

In order to compute the semiparametric estimator (2.25) a consistent estimate for is needed. Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez (2010b) and independently Shen (2010b) proposed estimating by maximizing the conditional likelihood of the 's given the 's, which is

(2.26)

When is absolutely continuous, the function in (2.26) denotes the bivariate density of the truncation couple. With interval sampling is constant, and becomes the first marginal density of evaluated at or, equivalently, the second marginal density of evaluated at . When is the maximizer of , it is easy to prove that the couple indeed maximizes the full likelihood under the semiparametric model. Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez (2010b) showed through simulations that the semiparametric maximum likelihood estimator (SPMLE) outperforms the NPMLE in the sense of the mean square error (MSE). This holds when the true truncation distribution belongs to the parametric family . When this parametric model is miss‐specified, the application of the SPMLE may result in a severe bias, so choosing good candidates for is critical. In the setting with interval sampling, Austin et al. (2014) suggested fitting a piecewise exponential model to the truncation distribution. Their decision on the number of pieces is based on an informal, iterative application of the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, while the location of the pieces is driven by the ordinary empirical quantiles of the truncation variable. Formal goodness‐of‐fit methods to assess the parametric truncation family were proposed and investigated by Moreira et al. (2014), who considered Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Cramér–von Mises distances for three couples of functions: , and . The null distribution of such test statistics was approximated by the semiparametric bootstrap that resamples the target and the truncation variables independently from and . Simple and informative goodness‐of‐fit plots can be constructed by a joint display of the nonparametric and parametric versions of the sampling probability . In our experience, a Beta model for the truncation limits is flexible enough in applications with interval sampling; this is the model we use in the examples of this section.

Basic asymptotic theory in the semiparametric setting includes the consistency and distributional convergence for the couple of estimators . These results can be proved by applying standard arguments, which involve the derivation of asymptotic representations for and as sums of zero‐mean iid terms plus negligible remainders. These conditions relate the smoothness of and imply the existence and convergence of the solution of the score equation .

Conditions (SP1)–(SP3) are standard in maximum likelihood theory. The interested reader may check the details corresponding to random sampling in Serfling (1980) or Lehmann and Casella (1998). The adaptation to the setting with doubly truncated data is straightforward. The following result is stated here without giving further details, some of which can be found in Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez (2010b).

Theorem 2.2.1   (Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez, 2010b). Let be a maximizer for (2.26). Under (SP1)–(SP3), with probability 1, and converges in law to a ‐dimensional, zero‐mean normal distribution with variance‐covariance matrix , where is the Fisher information matrix given by

The proof to Theorem 2.2.1 in Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez (2010b) reveals indeed that, as usual, is asymptotically equivalent to the centered iid sum . This, together with the regularity of the function , ensures the consistency and the asymptotic normality of the SPMLE. Regularity conditions for for one‐sided truncation were investigated by Wang (1989); similar conditions are needed in the doubly truncated setting, and we will not give further details here. The following result is stated under the vague assumption that the parametric truncation family induces a regular . A sketch of the proof is included in Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez (2010b).

Theorem 2.2.2   (Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez, 2010b). Let be a maximizer for (2.26). Under (SP1)–(SP3), and provided that is regular, in probability, and converges in law to a zero‐mean normal distribution with variance , where with

and

The limit variance of the SMPLE comes from the noise when fitting the parametric truncation model, , plus the variance corresponding to the estimation of under the observational bias induced by , which is . Indeed, when the truncation distribution is completely specified, equals , which is the limit variance of , the natural estimator of in such a case. It is interesting to note that, when is constant, reduces to , the limit variance of the ordinary ecdf. This is not surprising since is precisely the ordinary empirical cdf when is flat. The limit variance of the SPMLE can be explicitly calculated for simple parametric families. This is done in the following example, which serves to illustrate the efficiency gains with respect to the NPMLE too.

In the particular case of one‐sided truncation, the analytical computation of the asymptotic efficiency of the NPMLE relative to the SPMLE is possible. This is because an explicit formula for the limit variance of the NPMLE is available in the left‐truncated setup; see (2.20). We give now an example of such a situation.

Example 2.2.4    Let be a constant, and let and be independent random variables uniformly distributed on , so the cdf of is , , and the cdf of is , . From this Table 2.7 it is seen that the asymptotic efficiency of the NPMLE decreases as the truncation rate increases. Note that the noise attached to the estimation of is ignored in this example, since no parametric family is postulated for the left‐truncation variable .

For some particular parametric truncation models the maximum likelihood estimator may have an explicit form. The following example, in which the truncation variables are statistically independent, illustrates such a situation.

Example 2.2.5   (Example 2.1 in Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez, 2010b). Let and , , be independent random variables, so the parametric truncation density is , . Assume and . Then, , . The conditional likelihood (2.26) becomes , where

The estimation of the standard error of the SPMLE is easily done through plug‐in methods. Specifically, the Fisher information matrix is replaced by its empirical counterpart,

In the following example, the semiparametric approach is used to analyse the Parkinson's Disease Data in Section 1.4.5. A model is considered as parametric information on , after a suitable transformation to map the data onto the interval. The Beta model is appealing because of its flexibility; besides, it contains the uniform distribution as a special case, so it can be used to test for the stationarity assumption on the birth process, if necessary. Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez (2010b) investigated through intensive simulation studies the practical performance of the SPMLE when based on parametric Beta information, finding relevant improvements compared to the NPMLE.

Example 2.2.6    (Parkinson's Disease Data, Section 1.4.5). The performance of the SPMLE is illustrated with the PD Data (interval sampling). A two‐parameter Beta distribution to model the right‐truncation variable is considered. The observations are transformed so the interval on which is identifiable, , is mapped onto the interval.

For the late onset group the Beta model fitted to the truncation distribution gives and . The cdf and pdf of the fitted model are displayed in Figure 2.15. The SPMLE of based on the fitted Beta model is displayed in Figure 2.16 (right panel). The sampling probabilities used by the NPMLE () and the SPMLE () are depicted in Figure 2.16 (left panel).

A similar analysis has been done for the early onset group. In this case, the Beta model fitted to the truncation distribution gives and . The cdf and pdf of the fitted Beta model are displayed in Figure 2.17, while the SPMLEs of and are compared to the respective NPMLEs in Figure 2.18.

2.2.2 Parametric Approach

Assume now that the target is known to fall within a parametric family of cdfs , but no information is available for the truncation distribution . This situation is typically referred to as parametric setting, since the target is characterized by a finite‐dimensional parameter . From the viewpoint of the random vector the model is semiparametric however; indeed, it is possible to estimate in a semiparametric way once the parameter has been estimated. Anyway the focus of the present section is on the estimation of, and the inference on, and, thus, all the discussion falls under the umbrella of parametric inference. In previous sections we have seen that the NPMLE maximizes the conditional likelihood of the 's given the 's; this conditional likelihood is

where , see Eq. (2.5). Under the parametric model one has and the conditional likelihood becomes

(2.27)

where is the pdf of , and where . Maximization of with respect to leads then to the conditional MLE of this parameter, say. It is important to note that the marginal likelihood of the truncation values does not provide further information on . Indeed, under the parametric model the full likelihood is maximized by , where . Thus, is not only a conditional MLE, but also an unconditional MLE for .

Efron and Petrosian (1999) considered maximization of (2.27) under a special exponential family (SEF) in which the log density of is a normalized cubic function. Emura et al. (2017) carefully developed maximum likelihood theory for the SEF, and generalized the model by allowing an arbitrary polynomial for the log density; see also the computational results in Hu and Emura (2015). In these papers a simplified presentation of the required regularity conditions, as well as a detailed inspection of the parametric space, is achieved by considering the SEF. Dörre et al. (2021) followed the approach in Emura et al. (2017) to discuss the asymptotic theory in a location‐scale model for . Such a location‐scale model includes as particular cases three popular families, among others: the Weibull model, the log‐normal model, and the log‐logistic model.

The next result establishes the consistency and distributional convergence of under general, mild conditions, which should be checked in practice for the particular model at hand. In the following denotes the true value of the parameter , that is, . It is assumed that is a subset of the ‐dimensional Euclidean space . Conditions (SP1)–(SP3) in Section 2.2.1 will be assumed here for .

Theorem 2.2.7   Let be a maximizer for (2.27), and let satisfy conditions (SP1)–(SP3) in Section 2.2.1. Then, with probability 1, and converges in law to a ‐dimensional, zero‐mean normal distribution with variance‐covariance matrix , where is the Fisher information matrix given by

Theorem 2.2.7 can be proved similarly to Theorem 2.2.1. Note that there exists a duality between both results, in that the roles of the truncating couple and the target variable are interchanged. The next example provides an illustration of the parametric approach discussed in this section.

Example 2.2.8   (Parkinson's Disease Data, Section 1.4.5). The late onset group is apparently problematic in the parametric setup. For example, for the log‐normal model the MLE does not exist (the log likelihood is increasing in ), and the restricted searching of the maximum offers a poor fit to the data. This is avoided when using moment‐based estimators for and . Similar problems were found when using other location‐scale models for , such as the Weibull model.

Specifically, moment‐based estimators for the log‐normal model gave and . These moment‐based estimators are introduced by noting that, for the log‐normal model, and , where ; is replaced by to obtain the estimators. The estimates for the Weibull model were and . The pdfs and the cdfs corresponding to the log‐normal and Weibull models are displayed in Figure 2.19. For the Weibull model one has and , and this should be taken into account when constructing the moment‐based estimators.

For the early onset group, a log‐normal distribution (and also a Weibull model) was fitted by maximum likelihood. For the log‐normal model the MLEs were and . For the Weibull model the MLEs were and . See Figure 2.20.

2.3 R Code for the Examples

As is collected in Appendix A, there are some packages in R that include functions for analysing doubly truncated data. A brief (up to date) review of the available methods will be provided in the appendix. Throughout this volume, we will make use mainly of library DTDA, introducing functions from other libraries (specifically, DTDA.cif, DTDA.ni, double.truncation and SurvTrunc) when necessary. We refer to Appendix A (or library help manuals) for further details on functions usage.

2.3.1 Code for Example 2.1.8

For the Parkinson's Disease Data, we compute the NPMLE using Shen's algorithm for the age at diagnosis, both for the early and late onset groups, and the estimated sampling probability. Although the illustrations are done for early and late onsets, we will focus here in the early onset group. First, we show how to obtain the estimated sampling probability for the age at diagnosis.

> library(DTDA) 
> attach(PDlate) 
> res.late <- shen(X, U, V, boot = F) 
> plot(res.late$time, res.late$biasf, type = "s")

The NPMLE (using Shen's algorithm) jointly with the ordinary ecdf can be reproduced as follows:

> plot(res.late$time, res.late$cumulative.df, 
+ xlab = "age",type = "s", ylab = "cum. prob.", 
+ ylim = c(0,1) ) 
> lines(res.late$time,ecdf(res.late$time)(res.late$time), 
+ type = "s")

2.3.2 Code for Examples 2.1.11 and 2.1.13

This is the code for the examples dealing with simulated scenario I (no sampling bias) in Section 2.1.3. We will show first how the data can be simulated.

> set.seed(4321) 
> n <- 250 
> X <- runif(n, 0, 1) 
> U <- runif(n, -1/3, 1) 
> V <- U + 1/3 
> for (i in 1:n){ 
+ while (U[i] > X[i] | V[i] < X[i]){ 
+ X[i] <- runif(1, 0, 1) 
+ U[i] <- runif(1, -1/3, 1) 
+ V[i] <- U[i] + 1/3 
+ }}

The same simulation can be reproduced using the rsim.DT function in DTDA.

> set.seed(4321) 
> sim.data <- rsim.DT(250, 1/3, model = 1) 
> attach(sim.data)

The biasing function can be reproduced with the following code, and visually compared with the theoretical one.

> res <- shen(X, U, V, boot = F ) 
> plot(res$time, res$biasf, type = "s") 
> abline(h = 1/4, lty = 2)

The NPMLE using Shen's algorithm, and the target function , can be obtained as shown below.

> plot(res$time, res$cumulative.df, xlab = "X", 
+ type = "s", ylab = "cum. prob.") 
> lines(res$time, ecdf(res$time)(res$time), type = "s") 
> abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2)

The estimated biasing function and the theoretical biasing function for this scenario can be depicted as follows:

> res2 <- shen(V, X, X + 1/3, boot = F ) 
> plot(res2$time, res2$biasf, type = "s") 
> segments(0, 0, 1/3, 1/3, lty = 2) 
> segments(1/3, 1/3, 1, 1/3, lty = 2) 
> segments(1, 1/3, 1 + 1/3, 0, lty = 2)

Finally, the estimated biasing function and the true one, when the focus is on the right‐truncating variable , can be obtained with the following code.

> plot(res2$time, res2$cumulative.df, xlab = "V", 
+ type = "s", ylab = "cum. prob.") 
> lines(res2$time,ecdf(res2$time)(res2$time), type = "s") 
> abline(a = 0, b = 3/4, lty = 2)

2.3.3 Code for Example 2.1.14

For the simulated scenario II, which exhibits sampling bias, we can generate data with the following code lines:

> set.seed(4321) 
> n <- 250 
> X <- runif(n, 0, 1) 
> U <- (runif(n, 0, 1) ∧ 2) * (1 + 1/3) - 1/3 
> V <- U + 1/3 
> for (i in 1:n){ 
+ while (U[i] > X[i] | V[i] < X[i]){ 
+ X[i] <- runif(1, 0, 1) 
+ U[i] <- (runif(1, -1/3, 1) ∧ 2) * (1 + 1/3) - 1/3 
+ V[i] <- U[i] + 1/3 
+ }}

The same can be done using rsim.DT function of the DTDA package:

> set.seed(4321) 
> sim.data<-rsim.DT(250, 1/3, model = 2) 
> attach(sim.data)

The estimated biasing function and the theoretical biasing function for this scenario can be depicted as follows:

> res <- shen(X, U, V, boot = F ) 
> plot(res$time, res$biasf, type = "s", ylim = c(0,1)) 
> s <- seq(0, 1, length = 100) 
> Gs <- sqrt((3 / 4) * (s + 1 / 3) ) - sqrt((3 / 4) * s) 
> lines(s, Gs, lty = 2)

In this case, one may plot the NPMLE, the ordinary ecdf and the true .

> plot(res$time, res$cumulative.df, xlab = "X", 
+ type="s", ylab = "cum. prob.") 
> lines(res$time, ecdf(res$time)(res$time), type = "s") 
> abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2)

Figure 2.8 depicts the biasing function of the simulated scenario II and the true one with pointwise confidence bands based on simple bootstrap approximations of the standard error and some bootstrap replicates of the bootstrap biasing functions. For producing Figure 2.8, parallel computing has been used in order to accelerate the bootstrap sample generations.

2.3.4 Code for Example 2.1.15

The Equipment‐S Rounded Failure Time Data is an example of a rounded sample. We show how to compute the NPMLE, jointly with the ordinary ecdf.

> attach(EqSRounded) 
> res <- shen(X, U,  V, boot = F ) 
> plot(res$time, res$cumulative.df, type = "s", 
+ ylab = "cumulative probability", xlab = "lifetime") 
> lines(res$time, ecdf(res$time)(res$time), type = "s", 
+ col = 2) 
> plot(res$time, res$biasf, type = "s", 
+ xlab = "lifetime", ylab = "sampling probability", 
+ ylim = c(0,1))

2.3.5 Code for Example 2.1.22

For the Parkinson's Disease Data, specifically for the age at diagnosis in the late onset group, we can obtain the NPMLE using Shen's algorithm jointly with some bootstrap confidence bands. We may consider a percentile bootstrap method for . Note that it is also possible to obtain the pointwise confidence bands based on simple bootstrap approximations of the standard error.

> res.late.b<-shen(X, U, V, boot = T, B = 99) 
> plot(res.late.b$time, res.late.b$cumulative.df, 
+ type = "s") 
> lines(res.late.b$time, res.late.b$lower.df, 
+ lty = 2, col = "gray") 
> lines(res.late.b$time, res.late.b$upper.df, 
+ lty = 2, col = "gray")

As an alternative, pointwise confidence for the NPMLE can be also produced using the exact formula by Emura et al. (2015).

> library(double.truncation) 
> dt.late <- NPMLE(U, X, V) 
> q025 <- qnorm(.025) 
> upp.late <- pmin(dt.late$F - q025 * dt.late$SE, 1) 
> low.late <- pmax(dt.late$F + q025 * dt.late$SE, 0) 
> plot(X[order(X)], dt.late$F, type = "s", 
+ ylim = c(0,1)) 
> lines(X[order(X)], upp.late, type = "s", 
+ lty = 2, col =4) 
> lines(X[order(X)], low.late, type = "s", 
+ lty = 2, col =4)

2.3.6 Code for Example 2.2.6

The SPMLE is illustrated with the Parkinson's Disease Data, just for the late onset group. Note that, as a first step, values must be transformed so that they fall in the interval. This can be done as follows:

> attach(PDlate) 
> vars <- V-U 
> vt <- (V - min(X)) / (max(X + vars) - min(X))

Then, the observations are transformed to guarantee the identifiability of :

> xt <- (X - min(X)) / (max(X + vars) - min(X)) 
> xtt <- (X + vars - min(X)) / (max(X + vars) - min(X)) 
> resV.late <- shen(V, X, X + vars) 
> W.V <- resV.late$biasf 
> plot(resV.late$time, resV.late$cumulative.df, 
+ xlab = "age at blood sampling (years)", 
+ ylab = "cumulative probability",main = "PD late onset", 
+ type = "s")

In this example, we find a two‐parameter Beta model for the distribution of the right‐truncation variable , and for this purpose the log likelihood is given by the following function:

> loglik.beta <- function(a){ 
> result <- sum( log(dbeta(vt, a[1], a[2])) 
+ - log( pbeta(xtt, a[1], a[2]) - pbeta(xt, a[1], a[2]))) 
> return(result)}

Then, estimation of a Beta model is done as follows, considering a set of initial set of values.

> set.seed(1234) 
> par0 <- c(runif(2, min = 0.25, max = 32)) 
> res <- optim(par0, loglik.beta, method = "L-BFGS-B", 
+ lower = c(0.25,0.25), upper = c(32,32), 
+ control = list(fnscale = -1) ) 
> a.est <- res$par[1]; b.est <- res$par[2] 
> plot(resV.late$time, resV.late$cumulative.df, 
+ xlab = "age", ylab = "cum.prob.", type ="s") 
> vv <- seq(min(V), max(V), length = 100) 
> vvt <- ( vv - min(X) ) / ( max(X + vars) - min(X) ) 
> lines(vv, pbeta(vvt, a.est, b.est), col = 2) 
> plot(vv, dbeta(vvt, a.est, b.est), type = "l")

The SPMLE from the fitted Beta model can be computed and displayed with the following code:

> res.late <- shen(X, U, V, boot = F ) 
> W <- res.late$biasf 
> G.beta <- pbeta(xtt, a.est, b.est) 
+ - pbeta(xt, a.est, b.est) 
> F.beta <- cumsum(G.beta[order(xt)]∧{-1}) 
+ / sum(G.beta[order(xt)]∧{-1}) 
> pot(res.late$time, res.late$biasf, type = "s") 
> lines(res.late$time, G.beta[order(X)], col = 2)

If one aims to compare the semiparametric estimate with the nonparametric one, this can be done as follows:

> plot(res.late$time, res.late$biasf, 
+ type = "s", ylim = c(0,1)) 
> lines(res.late$time, G.beta[order(X)], col = 2)

2.3.7 Code for Example 2.2.8

As noted in Example 2.2.8, for the late onset group, the MLE approach does not provide a satisfactory approach for the parametric estimation for the log‐normal and the Weibull models. However, moment‐based estimators seem to work properly. Hence, reasonable initial values for the location and scale parameters of the log‐normal distribution can be obtained with a moment‐based approach for .

> attach(PDlate) 
> res.late <- shen(X, U, V, boot = F ) 
> W <- res.late$biasf 
> plot(res.late$time, W, type ="s") 
> mu.est <- sum(log(X[order(X)])/W) / sum(1/W) 
> s.est <- sqrt( sum(log(X[order(X)])∧2/W) / sum(1/W) 
+ - ( sum(log(X[order(X)])/W) / sum(1/W) )∧2 )

The log likelihood function for the log‐normal model is given by:

> loglik.ln <- function(a){ 
> result <- sum(log(dlnorm(X, a[1], a[2])) 
+ - log( plnorm(V, a[1], a[2]) 
+ - plnorm(U, a[1], a[2]) ) ) 
> return(result)}

The previous log likelihood is maximized as follows, considering as initial values for the parameters the ones obtained by the method of moments.

> par0 <- c(mu.est, s.est) 
> res <- optim(par0, loglik.ln, method = "L-BFGS-B", 
+ lower = .9*par0, upper = 1.1*par0, 
+ control = list(fnscale = -1) ) 
> res$par

The pdf estimator for the log‐normal model (jointly with the NPMLE) can be obtained with the code below.

> plot(res.late$time, res.late$cumulative.df, 
+ xlab = "age", ylab = "cum. prob.") 
> sx <- seq(min(X),  max(X), length = 100) 
> p.cond <- ( pnorm(log(sx), par0[1], par0[2]) 
+ - pnorm(log(min(U)), par0[1], par0[2])) 
+ /( pnorm(log(max(V)), par0[1], par0[2]) 
+ - pnorm(log(min(U)), par0[1], par0[2]) ) 
> lines(sx, p.cond, col = 2)

And the corresponding log‐normal pdf can be also obtained.

> d.cond <- ( dnorm(log(sx), par0[1], par0[2]) / sx ) 
+  / ( pnorm(log(max(V)), par0[1], par0[2]) 
+ - pnorm(log(min(U)), par0[1], par0[2]) ) 
> plot(sx, d.cond, type = "l", xlab = "age", 
+ ylab = "density")

One may proceed similarly for the Weibull model, whose associated log likelihood is given by:

> loglik.wei <- function(a){ 
> result <- sum( log(dweibull(X, a[1], a[2])) 
+ - log( pweibull(V, a[1], a[2]) 
+ - pweibull(U, a[1], a[2]) ) ) 
> return(result) 
}

The parameter estimates by the method of moments for this model can be obtained with the following code:

> s.estw <- sqrt(6/(pi∧2))*sqrt(sum(log(X[order(X)])∧2/W) 
+ / sum(1/W) - ( sum(log(X[order(X)])/W) / sum(1/W) )∧2 ) 
> mu.estw <- sum(log(X[order(X)])/W) / sum(1/W) 
+ + .57722 *s.estw 
> mu.estw; s.estw 
> par0 <- c(mu.estw, s.estw)

The NPMLE jointly with the Weibull cdf estimator can be depicted with the code below.

> eew <- c(1/par0[2], exp(par0[1])) 
> plot(res.late, xlab = "age", ylab = "cum. prob.") 
> sx <- seq(min(X),  max(X), length = 100) 
> p.cond.wei <- ( pweibull(sx, eew[1], eew[2]) 
+ - pweibull(min(U), eew[1], eew[2])) 
+ / ( pweibull(max(V), eew0[1], eew[2]) 
+ - pweibull(min(U), eew[1], eew[2]) ) 
> lines(sx, p.cond.wei, col = 2)

3
Smoothing Methods

Chapter 2 has mainly focused on the estimation of the distribution function, considering the NPMLE (Section 2.1) and the semiparametric and parametric variants (Section 2.2) as the reference functions for characterizing the behavior of the target variable . While the validity of such estimators is unquestionable from a theoretical point of view, the distribution function, being a cumulative probability function, may not reveal in a clear way some data features such as skewness or multimodality. These traits are usually better unveiled by smooth estimates of the density or the hazard function, which can be obtained by kernel methods.

Our aim in this chapter is to describe how kernel estimators for the pdf (Section 3.2) and the hazard function (Section 3.6) can be constructed in the doubly truncated setting. We also analyze their asymptotic properties and illustrate the performance of the estimators with some examples. Note that, in our particular context, the truncation pattern must be also reflected in the construction of the estimators.

Anyone familiar with kernel density and hazard estimation will be aware of the bandwidth selection issue, a non‐trivial problem that must be also accounted for. In Section 3.4, we present some selection bandwidth procedures for kernel density estimation when is doubly truncated. Bandwidth selection for the hazard rate will also be discussed.

3.1 Some Background in Kernel Estimation

We refer to Silverman (1986) or Wand and Jones (1995) for comprehensive reviews on kernel density estimation, but let us introduce some basic concepts that will be helpful for understanding the distinctive features that arise when is doubly truncated. Specifically, in a non‐truncated scenario, consider a random sample of , with unknown pdf . Denote by the ecdf obtained from the previous sample. The kernel density estimator is defined as:

(3.1)

where is the rescaled kernel ( usually being a symmetric density function), and is a deterministic bandwidth sequence such as as . For a fixed , it can be seen that

(3.2)

and, if , then the variance can be also obtained:

(3.3)

The mean square error (MSE) at a fixed point is immediately obtained from (3.2) and (3.3). From the expressions above it is clear that a value of reducing the bias will necessarily enlarge the variance. Hence, the MSE, which sums squared‐bias and variance, seems like an appropriate error measure whose minimization in (actually, the minimization of an approximation of the MSE) could lead to an optimal bandwidth value. However, such a bandwidth will be a local one, in the sense that it minimizes the error for a fixed . In order to obtain a global bandwidth, one may consider the integrated version of the MSE, namely the MISE (mean integrated square error), or even the ISE (integrated square error) as a starting point for optimal bandwidth selection.

Although the previous ideas seem reasonable, it should be noted that local and global error measurements to be minimized involve some unknown quantities depending on the density , which is the target function. The goal of bandwidth selectors is to provide data‐driven values for that can be used in practice. Bandwidth selectors can be constructed under two perspectives. On the one hand, one may explicitly derive the expression of an optimal bandwidth and then try to approximate the unknown quantities therein; these are the so called plug‐in rules. On the other hand, given an error measure, one may directly approximate the error expression and obtain the bandwidth value where the minimum is attained, such as in cross‐validation or bootstrap procedures.

In what follows, we will adapt the kernel estimator in (3.1) for a doubly truncated variable, and we will also introduce some smoothing selectors such as normal reference, plug‐in, cross‐validation and bootstrap bandwidths. Existing literature on kernel estimation for the density and hazard functions with different forms of incomplete or biased data includes Jones (1991), Cai (1998) and Zhou (1999), among many others.

It is interesting from both a theoretical and an applied viewpoint to investigate the bandwidth which minimizes the MISE, as well as the minimum achieved error. This can be done through simulations, where the unknown target and the nuisance parameters and are under control. Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez (2012) conducted intensive simulations to explore the aforementioned issues, and to investigate the performance of the nonparametric and semiparametric kernel density estimators. Among their findings we point out the following: (i) both (3.4) and (3.5) perform satisfactorily, reporting a MISE that decreases as the sample size increases; (ii) the semiparametric estimator is more accurate than the nonparametric estimator, provided that the parametric truncation model is properly chosen; and (iii) the semiparametric estimator requires a bandwidth smaller than that of the nonparametric estimator, according to its smaller finite‐sample variance. Here we further illustrate these points by simulating the scenarios I and II in Section 2.1.3.

In the simulations the theoretical MISE of can be approximated by the average of the ISEs along the trials,

where denotes the kernel density estimator (3.4) when computed from the th trial. The ISE of the semiparametric estimator can be computed in an analogous way. For each estimator, the optimal bandwidth that minimizes the MISE, , is approximated by the minimizer of the corresponding Monte Carlo approximation.

Example 3.3.3    (Simulated scenarios I and II, Section 2.1.3). We have computed the averages of the optimal bandwidth and the corresponding minimum MISE for the estimators (3.4) and (3.5) along 1000 Monte Carlo replicates of both models, with sample sizes or . The results are given in Table 3.1. For the computation of the semiparametric density estimator, as parametric information on the truncation variables we always considered a Beta() model for , with its support properly adapted to fit the () interval. Note that this parametric model includes the true truncation distributions in the simulation scenarios I and II.

From Table 3.1 it is seen that the MISE decreases as the sample size increases, supporting the consistency of the estimators. On the other hand, the semiparametric estimator is uniformly better than the nonparametric estimator. The efficiency of (3.4) relative to (3.5), defined as the inverse ratio between the corresponding MISEs, ranged between 0.73 and 0.79. Therefore, the asymptotic equivalence between and does not hold for finite samples sizes, for which the semiparametric estimator may bring visible improvements.

Even when the semiparametric estimator (3.5) can be recommended due to its relatively better performance, it requires the preliminary selection of a parametric model for the truncation variables. As discussed in Section 2.2.1, this is delicate, since an unsuitable truncation model may result in a large systematic bias of the estimator; see Moreira and de Uña‐Álvarez (2012) for further details and illustrations in this regard. In the following two examples we consider the estimation of the pdf for two real datasets. In both examples the Beta model fitted the truncation distribution well.

Example 3.3.4    (Childhood Cancer Data, Section 1.4.1). Two different bandwidths are used: (left plot) and (right plot). The two estimators are in good agreement. As expected, more bumps appear as the smoothing degree decreases. For large only two bumps remain, indicating the existence of two subgroups of cases: early cancer detection and late detection (less frequent).

For comparison, the naive kernel density estimator which does not correct for double truncation is also reported. We see that the naive estimator is close to the corrected ones. This is not surprising since, as we have previously seen in Figure 3.1, there is almost no observational bias on the age at diagnosis. Figure 3.1 also indicates the good fit of the Beta model.

In the next section, we will introduce some data‐driven bandwidth selection procedures. Some of the proposals will be directly based on (3.11), while others consider an approximation of an error measure to be minimized.

3.4 Data‐driven Bandwidth Selection

Expressions (3.4) and (3.5) require an appropriate bandwidth value for their effective application in practice. As noted in the previous section, bandwidth selectors can be designed under two perspectives. On the one hand, one may take the expression of an optimal global bandwidth, such as the in (3.11), and replace the unknown quantities there by sample counterparts. This first group of bandwidth selectors are known as plug‐in rules. We will introduce a normal reference bandwidth, the analogue of the rule‐of‐thumb by Silverman (1986) in the doubly truncated case; and a plug‐in rule following the ideas by Sheather and Jones (1991). On the other hand, one may directly consider an (estimated) error expression and then look for the value of that minimizes such an error criterion. This is the philosophy of other approaches such as the cross‐validation rules and the bootstrap bandwidth. In order to avoid unnecessary repetitions, we will restrict ourselves to the semiparametric estimator . The ideas in the following sections can be adapted in an obvious way for the nonparametric estimator .

3.4.2 Plug‐in Bandwidth Selection

3.4.4 Smoothed Bootstrap Bandwidth Selection

Another bandwidth selector based on the minimization of an approximated error is the bootstrap bandwidth. In this procedure the MISE of is estimated by means of a smoothed bootstrap since, as noticed by Silverman and Young (1987), a non‐smoothed bootstrap may yield inconsistent results.
