In the following section we illustrate the practical performance of the several selectors for the kernel density bandwidth through the analysis of simulated and real data.

3.4.5 Bandwidth Selectors in Practice

Moreira and Van Keilegom (2013) widely investigated through simulations the performance of normal reference rule, plug‐in, least‐squares cross‐validation and smoothed bootstrap bandwidths. They considered sample sizes ranging from to and different models with double truncation. The bandwidth values reported by the selectors were generally smaller for the semiparametric estimator when compared to those of the nonparametric estimator . This is in agreement with Table 3.1. Importantly, the bandwidth selectors were found to perform consistently, approaching the minimizer of the MISE, , for an increasing sample size. Also interestingly, even in situations in which the selector was not close to the optimal smoothing degree, the MISE of the resulting density estimator was only slightly larger than the minimum MISE. Regarding the relative behavior of the selectors, Moreira and Van Keilegom (2013) found an overdispersion for LSCV when compared to the other selectors; for this reason, the application of the LSCV criterion in practice may be risky. Another finding was the oversmoothing of the bootstrap bandwidth when compared to the plug‐in rules. Here we illustrate these issues by launching a set of simulated trials with sizes and from the scenarios I and II introduced in Section 2.1.3.

Example 3.4.1    (Simulated scenarios I and II, Section 2.1.3). We evaluated the bandwidth selectors and the resulting nonparametric and semiparametric kernel density estimators from 500 Monte Carlo trials with sample sizes and . For the semiparametric estimator we considered a Beta model for as in Example 3.3.3. In Tables 3.2–3.5 we report the median and the IQR of the 500 estimated bandwidths for each method and each simulated scenario, together with the MISE attained by the kernel density estimator along the simulated trials. For comparison purposes, the optimal bandwidth and the corresponding MISE are also reported. These values may be slightly different to those in Table 3.1 because the set of trials is not the same. Also, in one of the scenarios the MISE attached to the DP bandwidth is smaller than the minimum MISE; this is only due to the particular grid of bandwidths used when searching for .

From Tables 3.2–3.5 it is seen that LSCV and bootstrap bandwidths have a large IQR compared to the plug‐in rules, particularly for , and that the application of the bootstrap bandwidth results in some oversmoothing. The best performance corresponds to the DP and DP selectors. In general, the results are aligned with those in Moreira and Van Keilegom (2013), thus providing further support for their conclusions. For more detailed inspection of the results, in Figures 3.5 and 3.6 we report the densities of along the simulated trials, being each one of the five bandwidth selectors.

Example 3.4.2    (Quasar Data, Section 1.4.4). Following Moreira and Van Keilegom (2013), we apply the nonparametric kernel estimator (3.4), based on the five bandwidth selectors, to the quasar log‐luminosities. We also computed the biasing function to investigate the sampling probabilities induced by the double truncation for the log‐luminosities. The resulting kernel density estimators and the biasing function are depicted in the right panel and left panel of Figure 3.7, respectively. For comparison purposes, the naive kernel density estimator that does not correct for double truncation is also given (). It can be seen that the biasing function varies a lot, which suggests that there is substantial observational bias. In particular, adjusted log‐luminosities below zero are observed with a very small probability. From Figure 3.7, right, it becomes evident that, by ignoring the presence of truncation, a dramatically different kernel density estimator is obtained. Regarding the bandwidth selectors, the plug‐in methods (DP and DP) and the normal reference method (NR) give very similar results (, and , respectively), whereas the LSCV method () and the smoothed bootstrap procedure based on 500 bootstrap resamples (Boot, ) yield a smoother curve. As noted by Moreira and Van Keilegom (2013), a possible explanation for this can be found in the fact that the data are rather scarce near the left endpoint of their support (there exist only four observations of adjusted log‐luminosity below ). Note that, since the LSCV and Boot methods are based on resampling, it may happen that no data points are left in a given window when the bandwidth is small. This feature forces the procedures to select a larger bandwidth, and this might explain why the application of LSCV and Boot bandwidths results in oversmoothing.

Figure 3.7, right, also includes the nonparametric kernel density estimator based on 1000 resamples from the smoothed bootstrap (Boot2). In this case the selected bandwidth was , which means undersmoothing compared to the Boot method that uses 500 resamples. Therefore, the decision on the number of bootstrap replicates may also have some impact in the final shape of the estimator.

In Examples 3.3.5 and 3.4.2 we have seen how the naive estimator that ignores the double truncation may be grossly biased. In the following example we investigate how the naive approach may also result in a wrong decision on the optimal smoothing degree required by the corrected estimator (3.4). This illustrates how corrections for double truncation are also relevant in bandwidth selection.

Example 3.4.3    (AIDS Blood Transfusion Data, Section 1.4.2). In Figure 3.8, left, the nonparametric kernel density estimator (3.4) based on the various bandwidth selectors is depicted. The automatically selected bandwidths were (NR), (), (), (LSCV) and (Boot). All of them suggest a unimodal density for the incubation time.

For the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data there exists a strong sampling bias for the incubation time, as shown in Figure 3.4, left panel. This implies that a naive kernel estimator of the pdf will be grossly biased, as previously indicated in Example 3.3.5. Such naive estimation is depicted again in Figure 3.8, left. On the other hand, even when the corrected estimator (3.4) is applied, the result may be unsatisfactory if an ordinary bandwidth selector is employed. In Figure 3.8, right, the result of the latter situation is illustrated. Ordinary direct plug‐in (SJ‐dpi, ), solve‐the‐equation (SJ‐ste, ), unbiased cross‐validation (ucv, ) and biased cross‐validation (bcv, ) methods were used, resulting in a clear undersmoothing of the density. These bandwidths were computed by using the functions bw.SJ, bw.ucv and bw.bcv from the R package stats.

From the existing evidences one can conclude that the plug‐in methods DP and DP perform well in general, while LSCV shows a reasonable behavior but with a variance larger than that of the other methods. The performance of the normal reference bandwidth is also good, particularly when taking its simplicity into account. Finally, the smoothed bootstrap tends to oversmooth the density estimate.

3.5 Further Issues in Kernel Density Estimation

From a practical perspective, it is undoubtedly relevant to have bandwidth selection methods at practitioners' disposal, but the probability distribution of the target variable may exhibit more challenging patterns, such as presenting relatively different degrees of smoothing along the observation range. In this situation, global bandwidth selectors, which aim to provide an optimal degree of smoothing on the whole density, may not provide an adequate estimated curve.

When the underlying density requires different degrees of smoothness along the support of , the kernel density estimator in (3.4) can be defined with local bandwidths as follows:

The asymptotically equivalent version of is given by

As pointed out by Wand and Jones (1995) in their Section 2.10.1, the use of a local bandwidth is equivalent to considering a different kernel at each location. An alternative route to local smoothing is given by the nearest‐neighbour bandwidth, when is defined as the distance from to the th closest sample point. For practical computation, the parameter must be selected. A similar approach may be taken for the semiparametric estimator .

Kernel density estimation has been often used for data exploration. A relevant question here is which observed features are genuine from the underlying distribution, and not just caused by sampling artifacts. Some kind of uncertainty measure attached to the density estimate is needed for answering that sort of question. An issue here is that the bias of the estimator, and the fact that the variance depends on the unknown underlying density , hinder the computation of pointwise confidence bands for the pdf.

Despite these difficulties, some methods to quantify the variability in the density estimator are available. Simonoff (2012) suggests the construction of a variability plot based on the bootstrap, by computing the kernel density estimates from the bootstrap resamples along a fixed grid of points. Then, for each value in the grid, the 2.5% and 97.5% bootstrap quantiles are computed to depict a variability envelope. This bootstrap approach is possible with doubly truncated data too. The simple bootstrap and the obvious bootstrap presented in Section 2.1.4 are two appropriate resampling algorithms that could be used to this end, similar to what has been done for the cdf attached to the density .

Another option is to construct a variability band, as proposed by Bowman and Azzalini (1997), which aims to quantify the variability of the density estimate without accounting for the bias. In the doubly truncated setting, the key results on the bias and variance are given in Theorem 3.3.2. Note that the bias depends on , as in the non‐truncated case, hampering the constructing of confidence intervals. Regarding the variance, as done by Bowman and Azzalini (1997), one may transform by a square‐root; from the delta method, the corresponding variance is given by

(3.18)

which does not depend on , although it requires the estimation of and . This can be done nonparametrically from or, in a semiparametric setting, from . Then, for each fixed value , a 95% interval around is obtained in the square‐root scale by adding and substracting or, in the semiparametric setting, the amount corresponding to . In order to produce the final variability band, this is done for a sequence of values along the support of and, then, a transformation back to the original scale is applied. Note that such a tool does not allow us to examine hypotheses about a pdf (for instance, determining the number of modes), but it may be a useful graphical display for quantifying the variability of the estimator. In the non‐truncated setting, variability bands based on (3.18) present a constant width along the observation range of . However, for doubly truncated data, the effect of the sampling bias plays a role in the construction of the variability band, with wider areas located at undersampled ‐values.

Example 3.5.1    (Childhood Cancer Data in Section 1.4.1 and AIDS Blood Transfusion Data from Section 1.4.2). We have computed the nonparametric and the semiparametric kernel density estimators for the age at diagnosis of childhood cancer; the DP bandwidth was used. For these estimators, the corresponding variability bands based on (3.18) were computed too. The results are depicted in Figure 3.9 (left plot). The same procedure has been followed for the incubation time in the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data (Figure 3.9, right plot). Although no conclusions can be derived in terms of probability coverage, these bands allow us to explore the variability of the kernel density estimator both for the age at diagnosis (showing at least two distinct groups for younger and older individuals) and for the incubation time (with a higher variability at large values, directly related with their low sampling probability).

3.6 Estimating the Hazard Function

The hazard function, or failure rate function, is often used in Survival Analysis and Reliability to represent the prognosis of a patient or the performance of a device along time. For a continuous variable with cdf and pdf , the hazard function at point is defined as

The value indicates the instantaneous probability of the event of interest (death, failure) for the individuals or units still alive, or working, by time . In our doubly truncated context the hazard function is of course of much interest. In this section we discuss how to estimate under double truncation through smoothing methods.

The kernel estimator for the hazard function is given by

(3.19)

where, as in (3.1), is a rescaled kernel function and is a deterministic bandwidth sequence with as . The functions and appearing in (3.19) are the Efron–Petrosian NPMLE of the cdf and the corresponding empirical cumulative hazard, which is defined as

In the non‐truncated scenario, where is constant and equals the ordinary ecdf, (3.19) reduces to the ordinary kernel estimator for the hazard function (Wand and Jones, 1995).

The semiparametric version of (3.19), based on a plausible parametric truncation model, is defined as

(3.20)

Similar to the density estimation, (3.20) is expected to outperform (3.19) whenever the parametric truncation model is chosen in a reasonable way. These two different kernel estimators of the hazard function were proposed and investigated by Moreira et al. (2021).

Following the arguments in Section 3.3, the nonparametric and semiparametric hazard smoothers are asymptotically equivalent, and their asymptotic distribution coincides with that of the artificial estimator based on the true, unknown and . This is given by

Under the usual regularity conditions, it holds that and and, hence, the asymptotic properties of and can be derived from those of . These are given in the two following results, which were proved by Moreira et al. (2021). For the second result we will refer to the following conditions:

  1. (H1) The kernel function is a density function with , , and .
  2. (H2) The sequence of bandwidths satisfies and as .
  3. (H3) The functions and are twice continuously differentiable around .

Theorem 3.6.1   (Moreira et al., 2021)

(i) If is bounded on a compact support, is such that for each , is continuous at , and is a Lebesgue point of , then with probability 1.

(ii) If, in addition to the conditions in (i), is an even function, , has a second derivative which is bounded in a neighborhood of , and , then

in distribution.

Theorem 3.6.2   (Moreira et al., 2021) Under (H1)–(H3) we have, as ,

The formulae in Theorem 3.6.2 indicate that the asymptotic bias of the artificial estimator is not affected by the truncation issue, while its limit variance may be smaller or larger depending on the sampling bias and the particular point at which the hazard is being estimated. In particular, the variance is larger for small values of , according to the corresponding undersampling of the target variable around the point . Such an effect vanishes when is flat, where the usual expression for the variance is obtained. This fully resembles the situation of the kernel density estimator, previously discussed in Section 3.3.

As happens for the density estimator, the practical application of the kernel hazard estimator requires the selection of a bandwidth parameter . Following the previous ideas for density estimation, an optimal AMISE bandwidth can be derived. For that purpose, consider the MISE as the global error of ; this is given by

where

Under regularity conditions, the following asymptotic expression for the is immediately derived from Theorem 3.6.2:

Here the integral is restricted to an interval strictly contained in the support of , so it is finite. Interestingly, Hölder's inequality gives and hence, similar to density estimation, double truncation implies a larger overall error. Minimization of with respect to leads to the asymptotically optimal bandwidth

which is similar to (3.11), except for the integral appearing in that equation, which here is replaced by .

As it happened for the density case, the expression of depends on unknown quantities that must be estimated in practice. Alternatively, the LSCV procedure proposed by Moreira et al. (2021) can be used. With similar derivations to those presented in Section 3.4.3, the expression for the criterion applied to the semiparametric hazard estimator (3.20) is given by

where

is the leave‐one‐out version of . The optimal bandwith is obtained by minimizing over :

Similar to density estimation, it happens that the expectation of is asymptotically equivalent to (Moreira et al., 2021). This validates as an estimator for the optimal bandwidth. A similar cross‐validation approach can be introduced and justified for the nonparametric hazard estimator (3.19).

Moreira et al. (2021) thoroughly investigated through simulations the performance of the nonparametric and semiparametric kernel hazard estimators, the conclusions being similar to those already reported for the kernel density estimators (Section 3.3). Here we further illustrate the behavior of the hazard estimators by exploiting the simulated scenarios I and II introduced in Section 2.1.3, and also by analyzing real datasets.

Example 3.6.3    (Simulated scenarios I and II, Section 2.1.3). We take a modified version of the simulated scenarios I and II by considering a decreasing sequence of widths for the sampling interval: (which corresponds to the original simulated scenarios I and II), and . This means that the support of is , while . In principle, a smaller value of should result in fewer accurate estimators, according to the shortening of the sampling interval. This is not necessarily the case in our simulation studies, however, where the sample size of the simulated trials is forced to reach a pre‐specified value . As parametric information on the truncation distribution we take a Beta model for , with its support properly modified. For each model, we simulate 1000 trials with final sample size or 500.

The functions corresponding to the aforementioned models are shown in Figure 3.10. They basically resemble the situation of the original simulated scenarios I and II, with the corresponding shift downwards as decreases. In Table 3.6 we report the MISE optimal bandwidths and the corresponding minimum MISEs for the nonparametric estimator and the semiparametric estimator. From this Table 3.6 it is seen that the estimation error may sharply increase as the sampling interval gets narrower. In the most extreme situation with , the improvements in the semiparametric estimator relative to the nonparametric estimator are remarkable.

Example 3.6.4    (AIDS Blood Transfusion Data, Section 1.4.2). In Figure 3.11 the nonparametric (left panel) and the semiparametric (right panel) kernel estimators for the hazard of computed from the HIV infection cases are displayed. A Beta model was taken for for the computation of the semiparametric hazard estimator, and the parameters were estimated by maximizing the conditional likelihood of the truncation times, see (2.26). The smoothed bootstrap and the percentile method were used to construct 95% pointwise confidence bands for the hazard function. The LSCV bandwidths for the nonparametric and semiparametric estimators were calculated, their values being and , respectively. The two estimators are in good agreement, suggesting an increasing hazard, which is in accordance with the literature. For comparison purposes, the naive kernel hazard estimator, based on a bandwidth , is also displayed in Figure 3.11. This naive estimator ignores the severe observational bias for the induction time, see Figure 3.4, left, and uniformly overestimates the hazard function. This positive bias is a direct consequence of the roughly decreasing shape of ; indeed, it is easy to prove that, whenever is decreasing, the hazard attached to the truncated cdf is larger than that of .

Example 3.6.5    (Acute Coronary Syndrome Data, Section 1.4.6). As in Moreira et al. (2021) we use the Acute Coronary Syndrome Data of Section 1.4.6 for illustration purposes. For this dataset, it has been referred in Example 2.1.4 that the NPMLE does not exist or is not unique. For this reason we restrict the sample to the largest dataset on which the existence and uniqueness of the NPMLE can be ensured. Our final sample is composed by 917 patients, 680 male and 237 female, with ages at ACS diagnosis between 39 and 90 years.

In Figure 3.12 we display the nonparametric (left plot) and semiparametric (right plot) kernel estimators for the hazard function of , together with 95% pointwise confidence bands based on the smoothed bootstrap. The parametric information used for was again a Beta model. The LSCV bandwdith corrected for double truncation could not be used due to the non‐existence or non‐uniqueness of the NPMLE when computed from the leave‐one‐out resamples. Instead, the ordinary LSCV criterion was used, reporting bandwidths and for the nonparmetric and semiparametric estimators respectively. Ordinary methods for bandwidth choice are expected to perform well in this particular application in which the observational bias for the age at diagnosis of ACS is negligible; see Figure 3.13.

From Figure 3.12 we see that the two estimators agree in reporting an increasing hazard. The local maximum around 78 years suggested by the nonparametric estimator is a result of the large variance attached to , and cannot be taken as truly existing for the underlying hazard. This large noise of the nonparametric estimator is not surprising, due to the narrowness of the sampling interval ( years), being somehow avoided by the semiparametric approach, in agreement with the simulation study in Example 3.6.3.

3.7 R Code for the Examples

Similar to Chapter 2, we will now show and briefly comment on the code lines that will allow the reader to reproduce the analysis in this chapter. For this purpose, the library DTDA will only be used, given that it is the only library (up to now) that includes smoothing tools for density and hazard rate functions.

3.7.1 Code for Example 3.2.1

An initial transformation of the data is required. Note that this transformation will be used in all the examples handling the Childhood Cancer Data. Note that this transformation has been used for further analysis.

> library(DTDA) 
> attach(ChildCancer) 
> x <- (X / 365 + 5)/20 
> u <- (U / 365 + 5)/20 
> v <- (V / 365 + 5)/20

A parametric estimator of the biasing function can be computed considering a Beta model, as follows:

> lik.beta <- function(a){ 
> result <- prod(dbeta(u,a[1],a[2]) / (pbeta(x,a[1],a[2]) 
+ -pbeta(x-0.25,a[1],a[2]))) 
> return(result)} 
> par0 <- c(1, 1) 
> res <- optim(par0, lik.beta, method = "L-BFGS-B", 
+ lower = 0.9*par0, upper = 10*par0, 
+ control = list(fnscale = -1) ) 
> a.est <- res$par[1]; b.est <- res$par[2] 
> Gx <- pbeta(x,a.est,b.est)-pbeta(x-0.25,a.est,b.est) 
> wx <- (1/Gx) 
> wx <- wx / sum(wx) 
> F<-cumsum(wx)

A nonparametric estimation of the biasing function can be obtained, for instance, by computing the NPMLE using function shen and keeping the output in biasf.

> res<-shen(x,u,v, boot = F ) 
> plot(res$time, res$biasf, lwd = 2, 
+ type = "l", ylim = c(0,1), 
+ xlab = "age at diagnosis (years)", 
+ ylab = "sampling probability") 
> lines(res$time, Gx, col = 2, lwd = 2)

And once we have computed the NPMLE, we can also plot it:

> plot(res$time, res$cumulative.df, lwd = 2, 
+ type = "l", ylim = c(0,1), 
+ xlab = "age at diagnosis (years)", 
+ ylab = "cumulative probability") 
> lines(res$time, F, col = 2, lwd = 2)

3.7.2 Code for Examples 3.3.4 and 3.3.5

The code for both examples is quite similar. Note that the Childhood Cancer Data requires a transformation, as in Example 3.2.1 (it is omitted in the code below). We present the code for reproducing a nonparametric, a semiparametric and a naive (that is, uncorrected) kernel density estimators for a specific bandwidth value, . For the computation of the kernel density estimators, one may use densityDT in DTDA, considering semiparametric or naive weights ( wx in Code for Example 3.2.1, and wgNV).

> h <- 0.04 
> wgNV <- rep(1/length(x), times = length(x)) 
> resNP <- densityDT(x,u,v, min(x), max(x), 500, 
+ bw = h) 
> resSP <- densityDT(x,u,v, min(x), max(x), 500, 
+ bw = h, wg = wx) 
> resNV <- densityDT(x,u,v, min(x), max(x), 500, 
+ bw = h, wg = wgNV)

A joint plot can be reproduced as follows, with a suitable scale adaptation for the output.

> plot(resNP$x*20 - 5, resNP$y, type = "l", 
+ lwd = 2, ylim = c(0,2.5), 
+ xlab = "age at diagnosis (years)", 
+ ylab = "kernel density") 
> lines(resSP$x*20 - 5, resSP$y, col = 2, lwd = 2) 
> lines(resNV$x*20 - 5, resNV$y, col = 3, lwd = 2)

For the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data in Example 3.3.5, the following transformation is needed and the code above should be computed again with the new variables.

> attach(AIDS.DT) 
> x <- (X + 49) / 95 
> u <- (U + 49) / 95 
> v <- (V + 49) / 95

In order to compute a semiparametric estimator, a Beta model (as in Example 3.3.4) has been also considered, but replacing 0.25 by 0.57. Just recall that a transformation is also required for reproducing the figures.

3.7.3 Code for Examples 3.4.2 and 3.4.3

We will present the code for reproducing the figures corresponding to Example 3.4.2. The quasar data are also available at DTDA. Let's start by computing the NPMLE and exploring the biasing function.

> data(Quasars) 
> x <- Quasars[,1] 
> u <- Quasars[,2] 
> v <- Quasars[,3] 
> vxM <- shen(x, u, v, boot = F ) 
> plot(vxM$time, vxM$biasf, lwd = 2, type = "s", 
+ ylim = c(0,1), xlab = "adjusted log-luminosity", 
+ ylab = "sampling probability")

Now, we will obtain the kernel density estimator for the target variable using the rules proposed above: the normal reference, plug‐in, least‐squares cross‐validation and smoothed bootstrap. The different methods are clearly identified in the argument bw.

> vxDensNR <- densityDT(x, u, v, bw = "NR", 
+ -2.4, 2.1, 500) 
> vxDensDPI1 <- densityDT(x, u, v, bw = "DPI1", 
+ -2.4, 2.1, 500) 
> vxDensDPI2 <- densityDT(x, u, v, bw = "DPI2", 
+ -2.4, 2.1, 500) 
> vxDensLSCV <- densityDT(x, u, v, bw = "LSCV", 
+ -2.4, 2.1, 500) 
> vxDensBoot <- densityDT(x, u, v, bw = "SBoot", 
+ -2.4, 2.1, 500) 
> wgNAIVE <- rep(1/length(x), times = length(x)) 
> vxDensNAIVE <- densityDT(x, u, v, 0.58, 
+ -2.4, 2.1, 500, wg = wgNAIVE)

Note that in all cases we have evaluated the estimator in a regular grid in with 500 points, except for the smoothed bootstrap method, where a grid of 200 points ins considered. The results can be plotted just running the next code lines.

> plot(vxDensNR$x, vxDensNR$y, col = 7, 
+ type = "l", lwd = 2, xlab = "adjusted log-luminosity", 
+ ylab = "kernel density") 
> lines(vxDensDPI1$x, vxDensDPI1$y, col = 2, lwd = 2) 
> lines(vxDensDPI2$x, vxDensDPI2$y, col = 3, lwd = 2) 
> lines(vxDensLSCV$x, vxDensLSCV$y, col = 8, lwd = 2) 
> lines(vxDensBoot$x, vxDensBoot$y, col = 4, lwd= 2) 
> lines(vxDensNAIVE$x, vxDensNAIVE$y, lwd = 2)

For the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data in Example 3.4.3 the same code can be applied just being aware the transformation done in Example 3.3.5 both for computations and plotting the results.

3.7.4 Code for Example 3.5.1

Variability bands (semiparametric and nonparametric) have been computed for the age at diagnosis in the Childhood Cancer Data and incubation time for the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data. Note that both variables should be transformed as in the code for Examples 3.2.1 and 3.3.5. We will present the code just for the age at diagnosis in the Childhood Cancer Data. First, the quantity involved in the variance expression is numerically approximated.

> my.fun <- function(x) dnorm(x)∧2 
> RL <- integrate(my.fun, lower = -10, upper = 10)$value

The semiparametric weights based on the Beta model are obtained from a.est and b.est in the code for Example 3.2.1. The parameter is obtained from the semiparametric weights Gx in the referred code. For the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data, the 0.25 value in the Beta model should be replaced by 0.57.

> G.theta.inv <- function(t){ 
+ result <- 1 / ( pbeta(t,a.est,b.est) 
+ -pbeta(t - 0.25, a.est, b.est) )} 
> alpha.theta <- 1 / mean(1/Gx)

The semiparametric and the nonparametric kernel density estimators with DP bandwidth and the semiparametric variance in the square‐root scale are computed below. The semiparametric weights wx are those in the code for Example 3.2.1.

> seq.t <- seq(min(x), max(x), length = 500) 
> Gt <- G.theta.inv(seq.t) 
> n <- length(x) 
> dens.fit.theta<-densityDT(x,u,v,bw="DPI2", 
+ min(x), max(x), n=500, wg = wx) 
> h.theta <- dens.fit.theta$bw 
> var.t <- RL * alpha.theta * Gt / (4 * n * h.theta) 
> dens.fit <- densityDT(x, u, v, bw = "DPI2", 
+ min(x), max(x), n = 500) 
> h <- dens.fit$bw

The density plot and the variability band for the semiparametric estimator can be depicted as follows:

> plot(dens.fit.theta$x*20 - 5, dens.fit.theta$y, 
+ type = "l", xlab = "age at diagnosis (years)", 
+ ylim = c(0,3), ylab = "kernel density", col = 2) 
> sp.low.band.t <- sqrt(dens.fit.theta$y) + qnorm(0.025) 
+ * sqrt(var.t) 
> sp.upp.band.t <- sqrt(dens.fit.theta$y) + qnorm(0.975) 
+ * sqrt(var.t) 
> sp.low.band <- sp.low.band.t∧2 
> sp.upp.band <- sp.upp.band.t∧2 
> t.aux <- seq.t*20-5 
> lines(sp.low.band˜t.aux, lty = 2, col = 2) 
> lines(sp.upp.band˜t.aux, lty = 2, col = 2)

The nonparametric band requires the computation of the NPMLE for estimating the biasing function, which must be evaluated at the defined sequence of points (see code below). The corresponding variability band can be obtained just replacing var.n in the previous code by var.n.t computed in the code below.

> res <- shen(x, u, v, boot = F) 
> ind.mat <- matrix(0, nrow = 500, ncol = length(x)) 
> for(i in 1:500){ 
+ for(j in 1:length(x)){ 
+ if(seq.t[i]>u[j] & seq.t[i]<v[j])  ind.mat[i,j]<-1}} 
> Gn.t <- numeric(length(seq.t)) 
> for(i in 1:500){ 
+ Gn.t[i] <- sum(res$density.joint[ind.mat[i,] == 1])} 
> Gn.t.inv <- 1/Gn.t 
> alpha <- 1 / (mean(1 / res$biasf)) 
> var.n.t <- RL * Gn.t.inv * alpha / (4 * n * h)

3.7.5 Code for Example 3.6.4

Data must be transformed as in the Code for Example 3.3.5. The kernel hazard function estimator is obtained with the least‐squares cross‐validation bandwidth and including semiparametric and naive weights. Note that wx and wgNV are defined in the Code for Example 3.3.5. Pointwise confidence bands (nonparametric and semiparametric) were done using bootstrap resamples. Note that wx is defined in the code for the Example 3.3.5.

> vxM <- hazardDT(x, u, v, min(x)+0.001, 
+ max(x), 500, bw="LSCV")

The hazardDT function from DTDA can be used to compute the nonparametric estimator of the hazard function. The naive and the SP estimator are not included so far in DTDA, but the code below can be used to reproduce the SP hazard estimator.

> lik.beta <- function(a){ 
> result<-prod(dbeta(u, a[1], a[2])/(pbeta(x, a[1], a[2]) 
+ -pbeta(x - 0.57, a[1], a[2]))) 
> return(result)} 
> par0 <- c(1,1) 
> res <- optim(par0, lik.beta, method = "L-BFGS-B", 
+ lower = 0.9*par0, upper = 10*par0, 
+ control = list(fnscale = -1) ) 
> a.est <- res$par[1]; b.est <- res$par[2] 
> Gx <- pbeta(x, a.est, b.est) 
+ - pbeta(x - 0.57, a.est, b.est) 
> JJ <- sum(1 / Gx[1:length(x)]) 
> JJ0 <- sum(1 / Gx[1:(length(x) - 1)]) 
> FTETA0 <- matrix(0, ncol = length(x), nrow = 1) 
> WI <- matrix(0, ncol = 1, nrow = length(x)) 
> FTETA0[,2:length(x)] <- sapply(2:length(x), 
+ function(i) FTETA0[,i] <- sum(1/Gx[1:i-1])/JJ) 
> WgSP <- sapply(1:length(x), function(i) 
+ WI[i] <- (1 / Gx[i])/(1- FTETA0[,i])) 
> vec<-seq(min(x), max(x), length=200) 
> kdens <- function(data,h,x,wg){ 
+ w<-dnorm(apply(outer(x,data,"-"), 2, 
+ function(x) outer(x,h,"/"))) 
+ Mw<-matrix(rep(wg, times = (length(x)*length(h))), 
+ ncol = (length(x)*length(h)), nrow = length(wg)) 
+ sw<-as.vector(w\%*\%Mw[,1]) 
+ return(1/h*t(matrix(sw,ncol=length(h))))} 
> hazSP <- kdens(x,h=0.074,vec,WgSP)/JJ 
> plot(vec, hazSP, type="l")

3.7.6 Code for Example 3.6.5

In this example, the acute coronary syndrome data are considered. Note that just a reduced sample (namely ACSred in DTDA) is taken, in order to guarantee the existence and uniqueness of the NPMLE. Data must be transformed as is indicated below.

> attach(ACSred) 
> x <- (X - 38.8) / 50.4 
> u <- (U - 38.8) / 50.4 
> v <- (V - 38.8) / 50.4 
> tau <- 1.42 / 50.3 
> lik.beta <- function(a){ 
+ result<- sum(dbeta(u,a[1],a[2]) / (pbeta(x,a[1],a[2]) 
+ - pbeta(x-tau,a[1],a[2]))) 
+ return(result)} 
> par0 <- c(0.5, 0.4) 
> res <- optim(par0, lik.beta, method = "L-BFGS-B", 
+ lower = 0.9*par0, upper = 10*par0, 
+ control = list(fnscale = -1) ) 
> a.est <- res$par[1]; b.est <- res$par[2] 
> Gx <- pbeta(x, a.est, b.est) 
+ - pbeta(x-tau, a.est, b.est) 
> wx0 <- (1/Gx) 
> wx <- wx0 / sum(wx0) 
> F<-cumsum(wx) 
> res <- shen(x, u, v, boot = F ) 
> reshaz <- hazardDT0(x, u, v, min(x), 
+ max(x), 500, bw=0.021) 
> plot(res$time, res$biasf, lwd=2, type="l", 
+ ylim=c(0,1), xlab="age at diagnosis (years)", 
+ ylab="sampling probability") 
> lines(res$time, Gx, col=2, lwd=2) 
> plot(reshaz$x, reshaz$y, lwd=2, type="l", 
> xlab="age at diagnosis (years)", 
+ ylab="hazard function")

Regarding the semiparametric estimator, an analogous code to the one for Example 3.6.4 can be used. For reproducing the corresponding plot, must be fixed to 0.019.

4
Regression Analysis

Doubly truncated variables may be also involved in a regression setting. In this chapter we consider the case of a doubly truncated response variable and a vector of covariates , which may be categorical or numerical, continuous or discrete. First, as a distinct feature from classical regression models, the effect of the random double truncation in the observational bias is analyzed in Section 4.1. Two types of regression models are also presented in detail. On the one hand, Section 4.2 is devoted to the Cox proportional hazards model, which is the most popular model in Survival Analysis. On the other hand, the accelerated failure time model, widely used in reliability studies, is considered in Section 4.3. The previous models rely on the specification of a parametric form but, as for the density case studied in Chapter 3, smoothing methods can be considered for estimating nonparametrically the regression function too. This is done in Section 4.4.

4.1 Observational Bias in Regression

We consider a regression scenario in which the response variable is observed under random double truncation. As in the previous chapters, we denote by the pair of truncating variables, so is observed only when . Besides, a vector of covariates is attached to and, naturally, it will be available to the researcher only when is not truncated. Accordingly, the sampling information is denoted by , ; these are iid copies with the conditional distribution of given .

It is assumed that is independent of . Thus, the probability of sampling a particular value of is given by

where stands for the cdf of given , and where , as defined in Eq. (2.2). Equation (4.1) states that the sampling probability for is the expected value of conditioned by the event . When and are independent, the function is constant because does not depend on and, therefore, there is no sampling bias on the covariates. This is also the case when is constant. However, it may happen that some values of the covariate vector will be observed with a larger or a smaller probability. This should be taken into account if one estimates, for example, the marginal distribution of a certain covariate from the observed data. In its turn, the probability of sampling a value of is just regardless of the particular ; in other words, the covariate is unimportant for the sampling bias when conditioning on .

In order to illustrate these issues, let's consider two regression settings with a doubly truncated response : a regression model with a single discrete covariate (model RD), and a regression model with a single continuous covariate (model RC).

RD. A regression model with a single discrete covariate. Let be a binary covariate, , specifically with . Let be uniformly distributed on the unit interval when , that is, for . For let the conditional cdf of be , , for some real value . We take unless otherwise is indicated.

In model RC the transformed response fits a linear regression model with predictor and extreme‐value error term independent of the covariate. That is, where is independent of and , . Maximum likelihood here is applied ignoring the truncation issue. Figure 4.2 shows that the naive approach may be biased when the potential sampling bias is not taken into account.

In model RC, the sampling bias for under the truncation scenario II is small. This is because the function in (4.1) is roughly constant along , ranging between and . Therefore, not much difference will be found when comparing the ordinary ecdf of and the true, uniform distribution.

Due to the potential biases that can arise from random double truncation, proper corrections of the ordinary estimators are needed. Similar to the case in Chapter 2, unbiased estimators can be constructed by downweighting the multivariate observations with relatively large values of . For example, when is discrete, the conditional cdf at point is consistently estimated by

The numerator in , when normalized through the sum of the weights , can be regarded as an estimator for the so‐called subdistribution function . When is an event type indicator, such normalized quantity estimates a cumulative incidence function, as investigated by de Uña‐Álvarez (2020a). This is further explained in Chapter 5.

The estimator (4.2) fully exploits the independence between and , by using the same sequence of weights for each ‐value. Under the weaker assumption of conditional independence between and given the target can be still consistently estimated through the Efron–Petrosian NPMLE (introduced in Section 2.1.2) computed from the subsample , at the price of suffering from a larger variance. Obviously, such a conditional NPMLE can be regarded as an IPWE that makes use of some conditional weights . In practice, the consistency of the unconditional weights as appearing in (4.2) can be graphically assessed by plotting the curves for the several ‐values to see if no systematic deviation among them occurs.

4.2 Proportional Hazards Regression

The most widely used regression model in Survival Analysis is the Cox proportional hazards model, which makes use of the hazard function introduced in Section 3.6. The Cox model, see for instance Klein and Moeschberger (2003), indicates that the hazard functions corresponding to different covariate values are proportional to each other. More specifically, let be a baseline hazard function, and let be a vector of regression coefficients. Then, under the Cox model, the conditional hazard of given is

(4.4)

Therefore, is the hazard ratio which compares an individual with covariate to an individual with baseline hazard.

Mandel et al. (2018) suggested the following estimating equation for the model (4.4) under double truncation:

(4.5)

Note that the solution to Eq. (4.5) equals the maximizer of the usual Cox partial likelihood (Klein and Moeschberger, 2003) when there is no observational bias, that is, when is constant. In the general setting of random double truncation, a justification for (4.5) is given by the following result, which was noted by Mandel et al. (2018). The independence between and is implicitly assumed.

Proposition 4.2.1   (Mandel et al., 2018) Under the proportional hazards model (4.4), it holds

The asymptotic properties of the solution of (4.5) established by Mandel et al. (2018) include the consistency and the distributional convergence. This is formally stated as a theorem, where denotes the true regression coefficient. The following conditions are used in the statement of the result:

  1. (C1) is continuous and .
  2. (C2) The covariates are bounded and linearly independent.
  3. (C3) The limiting first derivative of is positive definite.

Apart from (C1)–(C3), the result in Mandel et al. (2018) is based on two conjectures: the uniform weak consistency of , and an asymptotic representation for the process , . Interestingly, both conjectures hold under assumptions (A1)–(A4) in Section 2.1.3; see Theorem 2.1.12.

Theorem 4.2.2   (Mandel et al., 2018; de Uña‐Álvarez and Van Keilegom, 2021) Assume conditions (A1)–(A4) in Section 2.1.3. Then, under (C1)–(C3), it holds that

  1. Equation (4.5) has a unique solution .
  2. converges in law to a zero‐mean normal distribution.

Rennert and Xie (2018) proposed an alternative estimation approach for the proportional hazards model with doubly truncated data. Such an alternative approach weights the terms in (4.5) by . These extra weights are not needed for consistency purposes, and they may result in standard errors larger than those corresponding to the solution of (4.5), as pointed out in de Uña‐Álvarez (2020b); see also Vakulenko‐Lagun et al. (2020) for further comparative analyses.

The solution of the score equation (4.5) can be easily computed in R by using the well known coxph function of the library survival, once the empirical sampling probabilities have been calculated. Specifically, the transformed weights must be included as an offset term within the coxph function. However, since the weights are random, the standard errors and the p‐values obtained in this way are no longer valid. In practice, the application of the simple bootstrap (see Definition 2.1.20) has been suggested; the simple bootstrap is used in the real data illustrations of this section.

Example 4.2.3   Consider the regression models with discrete (RD) or continuous (RC) unidimensional covariate introduced in Section 4.1. Note that these two models perfectly fit the proportional hazards model (4.4). We simulated 1000 Monte Carlo trials from each model with sizes and under the truncation scenario II in Section 2.1.3. This truncation scenario induces some observational bias, see Figure 4.1. The bias, standard deviation and mean square error of the solution of (4.5) are given in Table 4.1. For comparison purposes, two other estimators are considered: (i) the ordinary partial likelihood estimator that has access to the data before truncation (unrealistic, gold standard), and (ii) the naive estimator that maximizes the ordinary partial likelihood computed from the truncated observations. From Table 4.1 it is seen that the estimator that corrects the double truncation issue is virtually unbiased, although its standard deviation may be quite larger than that of the naive approach, particularly with a relatively small sampling effort ().

Example 4.2.4   (Parkinson's Disease Data, Section 1.4.5). Let's fit a proportional hazards model for the Parkinson's Disease Data in Section 1.4.5. Mandel et al. (2018) used a proportional hazard regression model to investigate the relationship between genetic information and age of onset of Parkinson's disease. Early and late onset groups are analyzed separately, in order to recognize if there is a distinct genetic mechanism that may vary with age. Both the PGC‐1a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) and the A10398G mitochondrial SNP were considered in a multiple regression model. Results are reported in Table 4.2. These comprise the solutions for the score Eq. (4.5), the standard errors estimated from the simple bootstrap based on 500 resamples, and the Wald‐type two‐sided p‐values. Statistical significance is found for both SNPs in the late onset group. Interestingly, this significance is fully lost and even misled by the naive analysis which ignores the truncation issue (‐values for SNP10398 G, PGC‐1a AG and PGC‐1a G indicators: , and respectively).

4.3 Accelerated Failure Time Regression

The accelerated failure time (AFT) regression model is often introduced as a log‐linear regression model (Klein and Moeschberger, 2003). Specifically, it is assumed that the log‐transformed response can be predicted by a linear equation where the first element of the vector is constantly equal to 1 and, accordingly, the first element of the regression coefficient vector is an intercept. Formally, it is assumed

(4.6)

where is a (standardized) random error term independent of the covariate vector and is a scale parameter. An alternative representation of the AFT model (4.6) is , , where is the conditional survival function of given and is the baseline survival, which is just the survival function of the transformed error . The term is called the acceleration factor, and changes the timescale from the baseline timescale.

The semiparametric AFT model leaves unspecified the distribution of in (4.6). Estimation of in the semiparametric setting can be performed by least‐squares. Under random double truncation, however, ordinary least squares may be inconsistent due to the sampling bias. A weighted least‐squares criterion that takes double truncation into account is given by

(4.7)

Of course, this idea also applies to transformations other than the logarithm, and even for an untransformed response. The consistency and distributional convergence to a normal distribution of the minimizer of (4.7) are immediately obtained from the results in Section 4.1 when and are independent. This was detailed in de Uña‐Álvarez and Van Keilegom (2021), who discussed extensions of the theory for a possibly nonlinear predictor and to M‐estimation too. Randomly weighted regression has been considered in other settings with incomplete information too; see for instance Stute (1999) for right‐censored data, or de Uña‐Álvarez (2003) for general biased sampling models. Each of these settings requires a specific sequence of weights replacing in (4.7).

The AFT model (4.6) has been more traditionally used in the fully parametric setting in which the error distribution is specified. In that case, maximum likelihood estimation is possible. The details of the parametric approach under random double truncation were recently provided by Dörre et al. (2021). In the parametric regression setting it is assumed that the truncation variables are independent of conditionally on the covariates , which is weaker than the independence between and . The conditional independence assumption is also needed for the alternative approach in Ying et al. (2020), who proposed a Mann–Whitney type estimating equation based on comparable pairs, so the possible truncation bias is removed. In the last few years other methods for regression analysis with a doubly truncated response have been introduced, and covering all of them would require a much longer chapter.

There exists an interesting connection between the proportional hazards model studied in Section 4.2 and multiple linear regression. Specifically, under (4.4) it holds , where is the cumulative baseline hazard and is a extreme‐value variable independent of the covariates. This general property shows in particular that the regression models RD and RC fit the linear regression setup, provided that the transformation is used for the response.

Example 4.3.1   Consider the regression models with discrete (RD) or continuous (RC) unidimensional covariate introduced in Section 4.1. These two models perfectly fit the AFT model (4.6) when a transformed response is used. Specifically, it holds with , and . The random error follows an extreme value distribution in this case; that is, , ; see Section 4.1. This distribution is not zero‐mean and, therefore, the intercept plays a non‐negligible role.

We simulated 1000 Monte Carlo trials from each model with sizes and under the scenario II in Section 2.1.3. Recall that this truncation scenario introduces a non‐ignorable sampling bias, see Figures 4.1 and 4.2. The bias, standard deviation and mean square error of the minimizer of ((4.7)), with in the place of , are reported in Table 4.3. We focused on the slope parameter . As in Example 4.2.3, two other estimators are considered: (i) the ordinary least squares estimator that have access to the data before truncation (unrealistic, gold standard), and (ii) the naive estimator that minimizes the ordinary sum of squares computed from the truncated observations. From Table 4.3 it is seen that, unlike the corrected estimator, the naive approach suffers from a systematic, although small, bias, and, due to its smaller variance, the naive method can report a smaller mean square error. This is similar to what has been seen when simulating the proportional hazards model, see Table 4.1.

We launched a new set of 1000 trials in the case ; the results are given in Table 4.4. A bit surprisingly, in this case the standard deviation of the minimizer of was smaller than the one corresponding to the naive estimator. This is interesting since it shows that the correction of the double truncation issue does not always results in an extra noise. In Figure 4.5 the sampling bias is illustrated.

Example 4.3.2   (AIDS Blood Transfusion Data, Section 1.4.2). Let's fit an AFT model for the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data in Section 1.4.2. We use a parabolic model to relate the AIDS incubation time (in months, variable ) and the age at infection (in years, variable ); that is, we assume . In Table 4.5 we report the weighted least‐squares estimator, the standard error approximated by the simple bootstrap based on 500 resamples, and the corresponding two‐sided Wald‐type p‐values. Results of ordinary least squares are included for comparison purposes. The fitted regression lines are jointly displayed in Figure 4.6. Compared to ordinary least squares, the regression line which takes double truncation into account is shifted upwards and depicts a more pronounced parabolic trend. The shift is in agreement with the sampling bias, which favours the observation of relatively small values of . When looking at the p‐values in Table 4.5 it is seen that, due to its larger variance, the corrected estimator is unable to find significance of the age at infection square at level 0.05.

4.4 Nonparametric Regression

Nonparametric regression techniques aim for the estimation of the regression function without imposing any parametric or semiparametric structure on the relationship between the response variable and the covariate vector . Thus, they are conceptually different from the methods reviewed in Sections 4.2 and 4.3, which were based on a proportional hazards assumption or on an accelerated failure time structure, respectively. Nonparametric methods allow for a preliminary, or exploratory, data analysis before any reasonable model can be postulated. Under another viewpoint, nonparametric procedures serve to get conclusions on the target population without any pre‐assumed structure that may compromise the inferences. Several nonparametric regression methods exist. In this section we focus on kernel smoothing, which has been already used in Chapter 3 to nonparametrically estimate the pdf and the hazard function of , and which can be easily adapted to estimate (Wand and Jones, 1995; Härdle et al., 2004). Due to the curse of dimensionality, which is one of the major drawbacks of nonparametric regression, we focus on the case of a one‐dimensional (continuous) covariate . Nonparametric regression estimators with covariates of higher dimension may converge slowly, and their application requires caution. Kernel regression methods with a left‐truncated response have been deeply investigated in the literature; see for instance Ould‐Saïd and Lemdani (2006), Liang et al. (2011) and references therein. Here we consider extensions of such procedures to the doubly truncated setup.

When is independent of , the observable conditional cdf of given is given by

Due to (4.8), the target can be written as

When there is no truncation, or when the sampling probabilities are constant, the estimator (4.10) reduces to the standard Nadaraya–Watson estimator. In general, however, the weights are needed to overcome the potential sampling bias; see Moreira et al. (2016) for further discussions.

The Nadaraya–Watson estimation is a special case of local polynomial regression, which proceeds by locally fitting to the data a polynomial of degree . Specifically, let be the minimizer of the weighted sum of squares

Then, is the local polynomial estimator of , adapted to the doubly truncated setting. When the estimator is called the local constant estimator, and coincides with the Nadaraya–Watson (4.10). When , the local linear estimator is obtained; this is explicitly given by

where , . In the standard setting of random sampling, is usually preferred to due to its smaller bias and boundary adaptability, and the same relative behavior is found under random truncation. The interested reader may find more details on local polynomial regression in Fan and Gijbels (1996), Wand and Jones (1995) or Härdle et al. (2004).

The asymptotic properties of (4.10) and (4.11) can be investigated from standard arguments when is replaced by the true underlying . Let and denote such asymptotic versions. As in Chapter 3, it can be argued that both and converge to zero in probability and, thus, the asymptotic bias and variance of and are valid measures of performance of the local constant and local linear estimators. Asymptotic expressions for these measures are given in the following result.

Theorem 4.4.1    (Moreira et al., 2016) Assume the following conditions:

  1. The second derivative of , , is continuous and bounded in a neighbourhood of .
  2. The kernel function is a density function symmetrical about zero, and with compact support.
  3. and as .
  4. The conditional expectations , , are finite.

It holds

and

where is the pdf of , , and .

Theorem 4.4.1 indicates that double truncation does not affect the asymptotic bias in nonparametric regression, since the formulae for the mean values are the ones corresponding to random sampling. The extra bias term appearing for the Nadaraya–Watson estimator, , is responsible for its poorer performance when compared to the local linear estimator. On the other hand, double truncation does affect the variance term; with random sampling, reduces to . Interestingly, may be smaller or larger than , indicating that more or less sampling effort around is induced by the double truncation. This is similar to what has been reported throughout the book for estimators of other targets.

In practice, computation of and can be easily done by using standard software for nonparametric regression, once the sampling probabilities , , have been calculated. For example, the function sm.regression{sm} provides the correct estimates when using within its weights option. As for the selection of the smoothing parameter , Moreira et al. (2016) adapted the direct plug‐in approach of Härdle and Marron (1995) and cross‐validation ideas to the doubly truncated setting. These authors showed by simulations that the bandwidth selectors perform satisfactorily, and that their relative performance varies depending on the regression estimator being employed and the particular scenario. Both direct plug‐in and cross‐validation bandwidths are applied in the following example. Note also that, as it happens for smooth density estimation, the consideration of a global smoothing parameter may not be adequate if the regression curve exhibits different degrees of smoothness along the covariate range. In that case, locally adapted procedures, such as those based on the ideas of nearest neighbours, may be an option (see Fan and Gijbels (1996), Section 4.2.1).

Example 4.4.2   (AIDS Blood Transfusion Data, Section 1.4.2). We have computed the local linear estimator and the Nadaraya–Watson estimator to estimate the regression function of the incubation time on the age at infection. The results are displayed in Figure 4.7. The direct plug‐in (DPI) bandwidths were 7.59 and 6.12, respectively; while the cross‐validation (CV) bandwidths were 20 and 14.4. Regardless of the bandwidth choice, both estimators suggest that there exists a concave relationship, with a maximum mean incubation time around 40 years of infection age. This is in good agreement with the parabolic fit in Figure 4.6. Likewise, the naive estimators that ignore the double truncation are grossly negatively biased.

4.5 R Code for the Examples

The code for reproducing the examples dealing with regression problems will be presented next.

4.5.1 Code for Example 4.1.1

We provide the code for computing the conditional cdfs for the age at diagnosis in the Parkinson's Disease Data, depending on the genetic information provided by SNP10398 (a similar code can be constructed for PGC‐1a). We will use packages DTDA and DTDA.cif.

> library(DTDA) 
> library(DTDA.cif) 
> attach(PDlate) 
> cif.late.z1 <- DTDAcif(x, u, v, 
+ comp.event = SNP_A10398G, method = "indep") 
> R <- cif.late.z1 
> p1 <- sum(R$cif.mas$cif.mas_1) 
> p2 <- sum(R$cif.mas$cif.mas_2)

The conditional cdfs can be plotted with the following code lines.

> plot(R$data$x[R$data$z == 1], 
+ cumsum(R$cif.mas$cif.mas_1)/p1, 
+ type = "s", ylim = c(0,1), 
+ xlab = "age at diagnosis (years)", 
+ ylab = "cumulative probability", main = "SNP10398") 
> lines(R$data$x[R$data$z == 2], 
+ cumsum(R$cif.mas$cif.mas_2)/p2, 
> type = "s", col = 2)

4.5.2 Code for Example 4.1.4

The code below present the code for plotting the ecdf of the age at infection (covariate ) and the corresponding marginal of the bivariate distribution for .

> library(DTDA) 
> attach(AIDS.DT) 
> res0 <- shen(X, U, V, boot=FALSE) 
> all<-sum(1/res0$biasf) 
> plot(sort(AGE), cumsum(1/res0$biasf[order(AGE)])/all, 
+ type = "s", xlab = "age at infection (years)", 
+ ylab = "cumulative probability") 
> lines(sort(AGE), ecdf(AGE)(sort(AGE)), 
+ type = "s", col = 2)

4.5.3 Code for Example 4.2.4

Proportional hazards regression can be carried out based on the coxph function in Survival. The results in Table 4.2 can be reproduced with the code below.

> attach(PDlate) 
> n <- length(X) 
> res.late <- shen(X, U, V, boot = F ) 
> W <- res.late$biasf 
> res.cox <- coxph(Surv(X[order(X)]) ˜ 
+ SNP_A10398G[order(X)] + SNP_PGC1a[order(X)] 
+ + offset(- log(W))) 
> summary(res.cox)

4.5.4 Code for Example 4.3.2

An AFT model is fitted to the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data, using a parabolic model to related AIDS incubation time and age at infection.

> attach(AIDS.DT) 
> res <- shen(X, U, V, boot = F ) 
> W <- res$biasf 
> xx <- seq(min(AGE), max(AGE), length = 100) 
> xx.d <- data.frame(AGE = xx) 
> res2<-lm(X ˜ AGE + I(AGE∧2), data = AIDS.DT, 
+ weights = 1/W) 
> p2 <- predict(res2, newdata = xx.d, se.fit = T) 
> plot(AGE, X, xlab = "age at infection (years)", 
+ ylab = "incubation time (months)") 
> lines(xx, p2$fit, col = 2, lwd = 2) 
> res2n <- lm(X ˜ AGE + I(AGE∧2), data = AIDS.DT) 
> p2n <- predict(res2n, newdata = xx.d, se.fit = T) 
> lines(xx, p2n$fit, col = 4, lwd = 2)

4.5.5 Code for Example 4.4.2

Regarding nonparametric estimation, consider the AIDS dataset in DTDA and compute a smooth estimator (local linear and local constant, with poly.index = 0) using the sm.regression function in library sm.

> attach(AIDS.DT) 
> library(sm) 
> res <- shen(X, U, V, boot=FALSE) 
> W <- res$biasf 
> res.LL <- sm.regression(AGE, X, h = 20, weights = 1/W) 
> res.LL2 <- sm.regression(AGE, X, h = 7.59, 
+ weights = 1/W) 
> res.NW <- sm.regression(AGE, X, h = 14.4, 
+ weights = 1/W, poly.index = 0) 
> res.NW2 <- sm.regression(AGE, X, h = 6.12, 
+ weights = 1/W, poly.index = 0)

The code for plotting the results (for local linear and local constant estimators, with DPI and CV bandwidths and for uncorrected estimators) can be found below.

> par(mfrow=c(1,2)) 
> plot(AGE, X, xlab = "age at infection (years)", 
+ ylab ="incubation time (months)") 
> lines(res.LL2$eval.points, res.LL2$estimate, 
+ col = 2, lwd = 3) 
> lines(res.LL$eval.points, res.LL$estimate, 
+ col = 4, lwd = 3) 
> plot(AGE, X, xlab = "age at infection (years)", 
+ ylab ="incubation time (months)") 
> lines(res.NW2$eval.points, res.NW2$estimate, 
+ col = 2, lwd = 3) 
> lines(res.NW$eval.points, res.NW$estimate, 
+ col = 4, lwd = 3)

5
Further Topics

In this chapter we consider a number of additional topics related to the analysis of doubly truncated data. An important issue is the adaptation of classical two‐sample tests for the potential sampling bias. In Section 5.1 we will see that ordinary methods may perform well under double truncation, particularly when the truncation pattern is the same for the groups being compared. Special settings in which the classical two‐sample test may fail will be discussed. Section 5.2 is devoted to the competing risks setting, of much interest in Survival Analysis and Reliability, in which several event types are present. Here we deal with two relevant goals: the nonparametric estimation of the cumulative incidence functions attached to the competing risks process, and regression approaches to investigate the influence of covariates on the cause‐specific hazards, or transition intensities. In both cases the usual methods must be modified by weighting the event times so the sampling bias is corrected, similar to previous chapters.

When and are dependent, the consistency of the Efron–Petrosian NPMLE is not ensured. Then, a critical issue is the detection of, and the correction for, the possible dependence between the truncating variables and the target. These topics are covered in Sections 5.3 and 5.4 respectively. More specifically, in Section 5.3 quasi‐independence tests based on association measures are reviewed and applied to simulated and real data examples. On the other hand, in order to adapt the Efron–Petrosian NPMLE to possibly dependent truncation, an approach based on copula functions is followed. In Section 5.4 we will see that handling with dependent double truncation is non‐trivial, and that the methods available at the time of writing restrict us to the scenario of interval sampling. This is an exciting area of research nowadays, in which several open problems remain; among them, the issue of copula selection, and the formal derivation of theoretical properties for the corrected NPMLE.

5.1 Two‐Sample Problems

In Chapter 2 appropriate tools for estimating the distribution of a target variable under a truncation scheme were reviewed. When is potentially influenced by a certain categorical covariate, it may be interesting to assess possible differences between distributions. We will restrict ourselves to the two‐sample problem, providing a brief literature review and illustrating through simulations and real data analysis how the classical rank‐based test may be affected by truncation.

Specifically, the goal is to test vs. , where is the cdf of the target variable in group , . In a non‐truncated scenario, classical tests were proposed by Mann and Whitney (1947) and Wilcoxon (1945) based on observation ranks, which indicate the position of the ‐values in the combined ordered sequence. The Mann–Whitney statistic can be alternatively introduced as a weighted difference between the hazard functions pertaining to the two groups. Specifically, consider

(5.1)

where is the weighting function and denotes the empirical cumulative hazard computed from the th group. Under random sampling this is given by , where is the group indicator for observation . The Mann–Whitney test corresponds to the choice . Equation (5.1) reveals that the Mann–Whitney statistic measures the departure between the hazards, paying particular attention to the ‐values at which the number of individuals at risk, , is large.

Some adaptations of classical two‐sample tests for censored and truncated data exist. For instance, Gehan (1965) introduced an extension of the Mann–Whitney test for right‐censored data, by restricting the jumps of to the uncensored 's, the so‐called Nelson–Aalen estimator for the cumulative hazard. Other choices for in (5.1) lead to alternative extensions of the Mann–Whitney procedure, like the one proposed by Peto and Peto (1972); or the popular log‐rank test, which is optimal to detect group differences under a proportional hazards assumption. See Klein and Moeschberger (2003) for alternative weights. In the same context Pepe and Fleming (1989) introduced as test statistic the distance between the Kaplan–Meier curves of the two groups. These ideas were also considered by Chi et al. (2007) for right‐truncation, specifically using an integrated weighted difference between the estimated survival functions. Also for one‐sided truncation Lagakos (1988) introduced a weighted log‐rank test for comparing two distributions. Gehan's idea was adapted to the left‐truncated and right‐censored scenario by Shen (2009).

The test statistic (5.1) was extended for doubly truncated data by Shen (2013), who suggested replacing the usual Nelson–Aalen cumulative hazard by the one attached to the Efron–Petrosian NPMLE. One interesting question at this point is whether the standard Mann–Whitney test is outperformed in this way. On the one hand, as indicated in previous chapters, the recovery of a doubly truncated distribution typically suffers from a large variance, and this may result in a loss of statistical power when testing for differences among the groups. On the other hand, even when the standard Nelson–Aalen estimator may be systematically biased under double truncation, the limit of the distance (5.1) could be larger for the biased hazards than for the true ones, advising against the application of any correction. Regarding the type I error note that, when the sampling probability is shared by the groups being compared, the usual Mann–Whitney procedure is well calibrated, since the truncated cdfs coincide under the null hypothesis in such a case. In order to illustrate all these aspects, in the following examples we analyze how the truncation pattern affects the calibration and power of the classical Mann–Whitney test.

Example 5.1.1   (Mann‐Whitney test, null hypothesis). Consider the simulated scenarios I and II introduced in Section 2.1.3, and let and denote the respective sampling probabilities for . Recall that, in these scenarios, is uniformly distributed in and . In scenario I, is uniformly distributed in and there is no observational bias, given that for ; whereas in scenario II, is uniformly distributed in , yielding a non‐constant , as shown in Figure 2.8. Explicitly, is given by , .

Simulations were carried out under . Specifically, two samples of the same size were generated from , according to the previous truncation conditions. Three different situations were considered: (i) the sampling bias for is in both groups; (ii) the sampling bias is in both groups; and (iii) the sampling bias is in the first group but in the second group. The proportions of (wrong) rejections of along 1000 Monte Carlo replicates for various significance levels can be seen in Table 5.1. In cases (i) and (ii), no matter the biasing function, the classical test performs correctly; see Table 5.1, left and middle columns. This was expected since, under the null hypothesis, the truncated cdfs satisfy when the sampling bias is the same in both groups. However, when observations from the two groups are subject to different truncation patterns, the proportions of rejections are much larger than the nominal significance level; see the right column of Table 5.1. This is because and are not equal in case (iii).

Example 5.1.2   (Mann‐Whitney test, alternative hypothesis). The ordinary Mann–Whitney test may hardly detect differences between and in specific settings. As an example, consider the simulated scenario I in Section 2.1.3 for generating a sample in a first group, so is constant. For the second group, assume that follows a distribution with a linear density for , and that the truncation pattern is that corresponding to scenario II in Section 2.1.3; that is, the sampling bias in group 2 is given by . Since is the uniform distribution in , it is obvious that . However, is almost proportional to (Figure 5.1, left), and this implies that the truncated cdfs and are almost equal. Table 5.2 (left) shows the proportions of rejections of along 1000 replicates when the target variable in group 2 is generated with density . In this case, as expected, the proportion of rejections is close to the nominal level, despite both distributions are quite different (see Figure 5.1, left).

The proportions of rejections become larger as the density of in group 2 moves away from . For instance, in Figure 5.1 (right), we depict alternative densities for the second group which depart from for small and large ‐values. Specifically, these densities are given by and . In this case the Mann–Whitney test exhibits some power, although it requires a large sample size to detect that . In fact, in Table 5.2 it is seen that, even for , the proportions of rejections are not close to 1.

As a summary of the previous examples we may conclude that, when the sampling probability is the same for both populations, any classical two‐sample test will generally provide reasonable results. Actually, when is shared by the two groups, there is no reason for conjecturing a better behavior of a test adapted for double truncation. As mentioned, the estimation of introduces an extra variability which may result in a smaller statistical power. Even more, the departure between the biased cdfs and could be larger than the one between and ; if so, a classical test would be even more powerful than the respective correction for double truncation.

Nevertheless, in our simulated scenarios we have also noted a deficient behavior of the classical Mann–Whitney test, both in terms of size and power; this applies to other ordinary two‐sample tests too. On the one hand, if the function is not the same in both groups, the test is not correctly calibrated. On the other hand, the test may present an extremely low power if but ; a situation that may also happen with different functions in both groups. In these cases, it may be worth to consider a suitably adapted test for handling double truncation. The log‐rank based test in Shen (2013) could be used for this purpose. Unfortunately, to our knowledge this corrected test is not available in R. Besides, its implementation is not obvious from the details provided in the referred paper, and this is why we have not explored its performance in the previous examples. However, we applied the classical Mann–Whitney test to the scenarios simulated by Shen (2013), obtaining competitive or even better results, both for calibration and power. This is in well agreement with our previous considerations, given that the designs considered in Shen (2013) correspond to the situation of a shared truncation pattern.

To sum up, if there is no evidence for suspecting that the biasing functions are different in the two groups, then the classical Mann–Whitney test should perform correctly, and can be recommended due to its simplicity. Actually, a non‐corrected two‐sample test may provide better results, in terms of power, than a corrected procedure when the ‐values at which departs from are oversampled, and this should be taken into account in practice.

In the following example we illustrate the issue of two‐sample testing under double truncation in a practical setting.

Example 5.1.3   (AIDS Blood Transfusion Data, Section 1.4.2). We consider two groups of cases: people infected when they were children (15 years old or younger) and infected adults. The goal is to compare the distribution of the incubation time in the two groups. The NMPLE of the sampling probability for the incubation time, , was computed for the two groups, and the results are displayed in Figure 5.2, left. This plot suggests that the truncation pattern is shared by children and adults and, therefore, the application of an ordinary two‐sample test is justified. In order to explore the departure between the truncated cdfs of the incubation time, and , relative to that of the true ones and , we provide the corresponding PP‐plots in Figure 5.2, right. The PP‐plot indicates that the truncated cdfs are relatively closer, although still showing a clear departure between the two groups. The expected power of a two‐sample test greatly depends on the estimation variance too. For this reason, in Figure 5.3 the ordinary (left) and corrected (right) empirical survival functions of the incubation time are depicted, together with 95% pointwise confidence bands. From Figure 5.3 it becomes clear that the correction of the double truncation issue entails a remarkable extra noise. As discussed above, in such an scenario an ordinary two‐sample test may be preferred to a test adapted to double truncation.

The application of the ordinary Mann–Whitney test reported a p‐value of when running the default option of the function wilcox.test. Alternatively, we obtained a p‐value from survdiff with rho==1, which implements the Peto–Peto test. Note that this is equivalent to the Mann–Whitney test in our application, because the data are uncensored. The conclusion of the test is that the children have a shorter incubation time.

5.2 Competing Risks

Competing risks data are often encountered in Survival Analysis and Reliability Engineering, among other fields. Competing risks relate situations in which more than one event type is present. In Survival Analysis, for instance, this may occur due to the identification of several causes of death; in Engineering, the separate investigation of two or more types of failure leads to a competing risks setting too. With competing risk, the event time comes with the event type indicator , which takes values within the set . Here, is the number of different event types. The event type indicator may be seen as a covariate in the sense of the vector in Chapter 4. This identification is convenient since, as we will see, much intuition for the construction of estimators is gained by applying the ideas and results in the previous chapter. However, should not be taken as a baseline covariate, because its value is only known at the event time.

Throughout this chapter we will naturally refer to the target variable as the lifetime or the event time. In the preceding chapters we have seen several examples in which a lifetime is doubly truncated due to interval sampling, and this may occur with competing risks too. This is the case of the Childhood Cancer Data in Section 1.4.1, which we take here as an interesting example of doubly truncated competing risks data.

Example 5.2.1   (Childhood Cancer Data, Section 1.4.1). We revisit the Childhood Cancer Data introduced in Section 1.4.1. In this registry several cancer types were identified according to the International Classification of Childhood Cancer (ICCC). We consider leukemias (ICCC group I), lymphomas (group II), central nervous system (group III), neuroblastoma (group IV), and other less frequently observed cancers that were grouped together (ICCC groups V–XII). Therefore, we have . In Table 5.3 we summarize some information related to these ICCC groups. Eight cases had missing information on the age at diagnosis () or cancer type () and were removed from the analysis; hence, the sample size is .

Example 5.2.1 is not the standard situation with competing risks data, which are typically recorded along a prospective follow‐up. It rather refers to registry data on children already diagnosed from cancer. This excludes the possibility of having a portion of the sample without the event of interest (cancer diagnosis), who would report a right‐censored value of at the end of the follow‐up. In other words, the analysis is focused on the distribution of (or on its subdistributions restricted by ) given that one will get cancer anyway. This is the situation by force, because no information on immunes is available.

A competing risks process is characterized by the cumulative incidence functions (CIFs), defined as , , . Under random double truncation these functions can be consistently estimated following the ideas in Section 4.1; see comments below Eq. (4.2). This was thoroughly investigated in de Uña‐Álvarez (2020), and the main ideas will be reviewed and further illustrated here. One critical point in the construction of the estimators is to assess the independence between the truncating variables and the competing risks process, which is represented by the couple .
