5.3 Testing for Quasi‐independence

Throughout this book it has been assumed that the truncating couple is independent of the target variable . This independence assumption is critical in the construction of the NPMLE, and also to establish the asymptotic properties of the NPMLE. In particular, the consistency of is not ensured when and are dependent. An alternative estimator of that takes the possible dependence between truncation and target variables into account is reviewed in Section 5.4.

Strictly speaking, a condition weaker than independent truncation is enough for the consistency of the NPMLE. This has been deeply investigated under one‐sided truncation (Martin and Betensky, 2005; Vakulenko‐Lagun et al. 2019), and some extensions for doubly truncated data have been studied too (Martin and Betensky, 2005; Shen, 2011; Austin et al., 2014). Actually, since the sampling information on is restricted to the region , there is no way to assess the independence between and on their whole supports. At maximum, one will see that the truncating couple and the target variable behave in the observable region as if they were independent in the unobservable world. This has been termed quasi‐independence in the literature on randomly truncated data. For one‐sided truncation Vakulenko‐Lagun et al. (2019) justified that the Lynden‐Bell estimator (Lynden–Bell, 1971) is consistent merely under quasi‐independence. Moreover, they revealed and discussed a non‐identifiability aspect of quasi‐independence that had been unnoticed up to then. Similar issues appear by force under double truncation, which is an extension of the one‐sided truncation setup.

Several tests for quasi‐independence with doubly truncated data have been proposed; the literature includes Efron and Petrosian (1999), Martin and Betensky (2005) and Shen (2011). In this section we briefly present the conditional Kendall's Tau method introduced by Martin and Betensky (2005) and later revisited by Austin et al. (2014). This method is implemented in the R package SurvTrunc.

For ease of presentation we focus on interval sampling, which is the most important scenario of doubly truncated data, and where the couple falls on a line with probability one. In such a case it is enough to measure the association between and . The conditional Kendall's Tau is defined as

(5.8)

where with . The Kendall's Tau (5.8) measures the association between and by using the couples of observations that are comparable. In practice, can be much smaller than the total amount of couples, . Importantly, due to the double truncation effects, the strength of the association that is measured through (5.8) may be weaker than the one existing in the unobservable world. This should be taken into account when interpreting empirical results.

Under the null hypothesis of quasi‐independence, converges in distribution to a as . The asymptotic variance of (5.8) can be easily estimated from the data, as discussed in Section 6 of Martin and Betensky (2005). A chi‐squared test statistic with one degree of freedom is thus given by ; that is, quasi‐independence is rejected when the ‐value is below the nominal level. When the truncating variables and do not determine each other, a chi‐squared test with two degrees of freedom can be constructed in a similar way. In such a case, the test statistic involves two conditional association measures, corresponding to and combinations (Martin and Betensky, 2005).

This could result in a positive dependence between the recorded incubation time and ; note that is essentially the date of infection. In Moreira et al. In this case, the conditional Kendall's Tau is , and it is based on 18059 comparable couples of observations (about 22% of the total). 5.4 Dependent Truncation

In the previous section we discussed how to assess the assumption of independent truncation. When independent truncation is rejected, or when there exists external information on the association between the truncating variables and the target , methods alternative to the Efron–Petrosian NPMLE are needed. In this section we review a recent approach based on copulas for the estimation of a doubly truncated cdf under possibly dependent truncation. This extends copula‐based estimation under dependent one‐sided truncation (Emura and Wang, 2012) to the doubly truncated setting. See Chiou et al. (2019) for alternative ideas to deal with dependent truncation via transformation models.

Copula functions (Nelsen, 2006) have been often used in statistics to handle dependence in a number of settings. In particular, in Survival Analysis copulas have served to model the issues of dependent censoring and dependent truncation. The copula‐based approach starts by splitting a multivariate distribution of interest into two components: (i) the marginal distributions, and (ii) the link among the margins. How to estimate both components depends on the particular setting one is working with.

Similar to the case in Section 5.3, for ease of presentation we consider the situation of interval sampling, in which double truncation is induced by a single truncating variable , because for a known positive constant . This has been carefully studied by Moreira et al. (2021). For the alternative scenario in which the couple is not concentrated on a line, a similar approach is in principle possible, with the extra complexity entailed by the multivariate nature of the truncation variable. The details of such an extension are however missing in the related literature.

A copula function is a bivariate distribution on the unit square with uniform margins. Let denote the bivariate cdf of , and let and be its margins. As in previous chapters we denote by and the respective supports of and . According to Sklar's theorem (Nelsen, 2006), there exists a copula function such that

Furthermore, if and are continuous, the copula is unique. When , , the variables and are independent but, otherwise, they are dependent. The association between and induced by a given copula function is often measured through the Kendall's Tau, which is given by

Dependent truncation can be handled in a relatively easy way through a copula model indexed by a univariate or multivariate parameter . Plenty of examples are given in Nelsen (2006). Here we only quote three of them for illustration purposes; in the following we put for :

  1. C1. Clayton copula: , . Kendall's Tau: .
  2. C2. Frank copula: , . Kendall's Tau: , where is the Debye function of the first kind.
  3. C3. Farlie–Gumbel–Morgenstern (FGM) copula: , . Kendall's Tau: .

Clayton, Frank and FGM copulas have the independent copula as a special (limiting) case (). Given a copula family , the copula parameter and the margins and can be estimated by maximum likelihood principles. Details are given below.

In Figure 5.10 we depict scatterplots of couples simulated from the Clayton copula with three different association degrees. Dependence is hardly guessed when , but it is clearly seen when the Kendall's Tau is 0.5 or larger. In Figure 5.11 the scatterplots correspond to the copula families C1 and C2; the Kendall's Tau is 0.9 in the two cases. From Figure 5.11 it is seen how different copula functions will induce different dependence patterns. This should be taken into account when choosing a particular copula family to model the dependent truncation.

A non‐trivial issue in copula‐based estimation from incomplete data is the identifiability of the copula. That is, before introducing an estimator for , one should guarantee that two different ‐values cannot generate the same distribution for in the observable region . This leads to the following definition. Let denote the second‐order derivative of with respect to its two arguments.

Definition 5.4.1    (Moreira et al., 2021) A copula family is called double truncated identifiable if, for , , a constant , and differentiable non‐decreasing functions and , equality

in an open set in , with non‐decreasing functions on , implies that , , and .

Moreira et al. (2021) proved that the identifiability condition in Definition 5.4.1 is enough in the setting of interval sampling. In other words, they proved that, under the condition in Definition 5.4.1, two different triplets by force induce different joint distributions for in the observable region. Copula families C1–C3 above are examples of copulas that satisfy Definition 5.4.1.

When and are linked through a copula function , the joint pdf of the observable , with , is proportional to , , , , where and denote the pdf of and , respectively. In order to derive the likelihood of the sample , , we proceed as in Chapter 2 by assuming that and are concentrated respectively on the 's and 's, with masses and , . Introduce

and , where . With this notation the likelihood can be written as

with and . For the independence copula , , it holds for and, hence, the likelihood (5.9) reduces to the one in Chapter 2, see Eq. (2.4).

Moreira et al. (2021) introduced two different iterative algorithms to maximize the likelihood (5.9) for a given parametric copula family . These two algorithms are termed simple and full in the referred paper. Both algorithms iterate up to reaching a solution for the score equations that arise from the first partial derivatives of the log likelihood with respect to , and . The difference between the two algorithms is in the computation of the partial derivatives. The simple algorithm deals with as if it were free of and , thus leading to relatively plain score equations. In its turn, the full algorithm computes the partial derivatives by taking into account the fact that actually involves both and ; the score equations are of course more involved in this case. One interesting finding in Moreira et al. (2021) is that the simple algorithm behaves in a competitive way, while saving computational time. Both the simple and the full algorithms end with an estimator of the triplet . The bivariate cdf of at point can be then estimated by .

By using the aforementioned approach of the simple algorithm, the following score equations are immediately obtained:

Given a parametric copula family , the simple algorithm as introduced in Moreira et al. (2021) proceeds as follows:

  1. SA1. Take , where and are initial solutions for and .
  2. SA2. Use (5.11) to improve and get , say; that is, use and to compute in (5.11).
  3. SA3. Use (5.10) to improve and get , say; that is, use and to compute in (5.10).
  4. SA4. Compute .

In steps SA2 and SA3 the are computed from the same triplet . Steps SA2–SA4 are repeated until reaching convergence.

Example 5.4.2   (Simulated scenario I in Section 2.1.3 with dependent truncation). For illustration purposes we introduce dependent truncation in the simulated scenario I, Section 2.1.3, through Clayton and Frank copulas, with in both cases. In Figure 5.12 the NPMLE computed from a single trial of size simulated from each copula model is displayed. From this Figure 5.12 it is seen that the Efron–Petrosian that ignores the dependent truncation is grossly biased; this is particularly visible for the Frank copula. On the other hand, the NPMLE based on the true copula family, fitted with the estimated , approximates the target well.

In the next example we apply the simple algorithm SA1–SA4 to two real datasets: the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data of Section 1.4.2, and the Childhood Cancer Data of Section 1.4.1. Copula families C1–C3 above are used in the example. For each copula, the standard error of is approximated by bootstrapping. For this, the copula‐based obvious bootstrap proposed by Moreira et al. (2021) is applied. This method proceeds as follows:

  1. CB1. Draw a couple of uniform random variables from .
  2. CB2. Do and , where and are the quantile functions of the copula‐based NPMLEs of and .
  3. CB3. Repeat step CB2 until is fulfilled.

Nelsen (2006) provides simulation algorithms for specific copula families that can be used in step CB1.

Example 5.4.3   (AIDS Blood Transfusion Data. Section 1.4.2 and Childhood Cancer Data, Section 1.4.1). FGM, Clayton and Frank copula families were fitted to the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data and the Childhood Cancer Data by using the simple algorithm SA1–SA4. As explained in Section 5.3, a positive association is expected in the former case, but not for the Childhood Cancer Data. This is confirmed by the results of the copula‐based analysis, see Table 5.6. For the AIDS data, Kendall's Tau for FGM, Clayton and Frank copulas was 0.22, 0.20 and 0.38 respectively. Importantly, the 95% confidence intervals for based on the semiparametric bootstrap CB1–CB3 and the normal approximation exclude the independence value for the three copula families. In Figure 5.13 the NPMLEs based on FGM, Clayton, Frank and independence copulas are displayed. From this Figure 5.13 it is seen that the copula‐based estimators are close to the Efron–Petrosian NPMLE for the Childhood Cancer Data, while they introduce a noticeable shift for the AIDS Data. This is particularly true for the Frank‐based estimator, which detects the largest association between and .

In order to illustrate the simple algorithm, in Figure 5.14 we depict the logarithm of (5.9) for the AIDS Blood Transfusion Data and the three copula families. For each copula two functions are displayed: (i) the one corresponding to the initial solution , and (ii) the one corresponding to the final solution of the algorithm SA1–SA4. From this Figure 5.14 it is seen how the log likelihood function changes along the iterations.

In Moreira et al. (2021) the performance of the algorithm SA1–SA4, together with that of the alternative full algorithm, was thoroughly investigated through simulations. The estimators performed accurately in the simulated scenarios in that paper, supporting the copula‐based approach for dependent double truncation. Still, numerical instabilities may appear due to the sensitiveness of the algorithm with respect to the initial solution, or the existence of local maxima. Further investigation of these issues is required in order to improve the robustness of the procedures.

5.5 R Code for the Examples

The code for reproducing some of the examples in this chapter is presented below. As in previous chapters, DTDA package will be the reference, but we will also make use of other packages.

5.5.1 Code for Example 5.1.3

In this example, the goal was to compare the distribution of the incubation time for children vs. people older than 15 years.

> attach(AIDS.DT) 
> Z <- as.numeric(AGE <= 15) 
> res <- wilcox.test(X ˜ AGE <= 15) 
> F0 <- shen(X[Z==0], U[Z==0], V[Z==0], boot = F) 
> F1 <- shen(X[Z==1], U[Z==1], V[Z==1], boot = F)

NPMLE estimators of both groups can be plotted for visual comparison.

> plot(F0$time, F0$biasf, type = "s", ylim = c(0,1), 
+ xlab = "incubation time (months)", 
+ ylab = "sampling probability") 
> lines(F1$time, F1$biasf, type = "s", col = 2)

A PP‐plot for the ordinary and the corrected estimators can be computed as follows:

> xpool <- c(F0$time, F1$time) 
> plot(ecdf(X[Z==0])(xpool), ecdf(X[Z==1])(xpool), 
> xlab = "cumulative probability, adults", 
> ylab = "cumulative probability, children") 
> abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = 2) 
> nn <- length(xpool) 
> F0c <- rep(-1, nn); F1c <- F0c 
> for (i in 1:nn){ 
+ F0c[i] <- max(F0$cumulative.df[F0$time <= xpool[i]]) 
+ F1c[i] <- max(F1$cumulative.df[F1$time <= xpool[i]])} 
> F1c[F1c == -Inf] <- 0 
> points(F0c, F1c, pch = 3)

The ordinary ecdf jointly with a pointwise band can be produced using survdiff and survfit in package survival.

> library(survival) 
> logrank <- survdiff(Surv(X) ˜ Z) 
> peto <- survdiff(Surv(X) ˜ Z, rho = 1) 
> km <- survfit(Surv(X)˜ Z, conf.type = "plain") 
> plot(km, col = 1:2, conf.int = T, 
+ xlab = "incubation time (months)", 
+ ylab = "survival probability")

Finally, the NPMLE with pointwise confidence bands based on a normal approximation with bootstrap standard errors are also useful for comparing the two groups.

> F0 <- shen(X[Z==0], U[Z==0], V[Z==0], boot = T) 
> F1 <- shen(X[Z==1], U[Z==1], V[Z==1], boot = T) 
> plot(F0$time, 1 - F0$cumulative.df, type = "s", 
+ xlab = "incubation time (months)", ylab = "") 
> upp0.try <- pmin(F0$cumulative.df - qnorm(0.975) 
+ * F0$sd.boot, 1) 
> low0.try <- pmax(F0$cumulative.df + qnorm(0.975) 
+ * F0$sd.boot, 0) 
> upp1.try <- pmin(F1$cumulative.df - qnorm(0.975) 
+ * F1$sd.boot, 1) 
> low1.try <- pmax(F1$cumulative.df + qnorm(0.975) 
+ * F1$sd.boot, 0) 
> lines(F0$time, 1 - upp0.try, type = "s", lty = 2) 
> lines(F0$time, 1- low0.try, type = "s", lty = 2) 
> lines(F1$time, 1- F1$cumulative.df, type = "s", 
+ col = 2) 
> lines(F1$time, 1 - upp1.try, type = "s", lty = 2, 
+ col = 2) 
> lines(F1$time, 1 - low1.try, type = "s", lty = 2, 
+ col = 2)

5.5.2 Code for Example 5.2.4

We make use of both DTDA and DTDA.cif in this example. We present the procedure just for one of the groups, specifically, ICCGroup equal to 1. The same analysis can be repeated for the other groups (that is ICCGroup equal to 2, 3, 4 and larger or equal to 5).

> library(DTDA.cif) 
> attach(ChildCancer) 
> Ch<-ChildCancer[!is.na(ICCGroup),] 
> attach(Ch) 
> Ch1<-subset(ChildCancer, ICCGroup == 1) 
> x1 <- Ch1$X; u1 <- Ch1$U; v1 <- Ch1$V 
> res1 <- DTDAcif(x1, u1, v1) 
> plot(sort(x1), res1$biasf, type = "s", ylim = c(0,1)) 
> w1 <- 1 / res1$biasf

Weights for independent truncation are computed as follows:

> res <- DTDAcif(X, U, V) 
> w <- 1 / res$biasf 
> w <- w / sum(w) 
> w01 <- w * as.numeric(ICCGroup==1)

The sampling bias can be visualized with the code below.

> plot(x1[order(x1)]/365, res1$biasf, type = "s", 
+ ylim = c(0,1), xlim = c(min(X/365),max(X/365)), 
+ ylab = "sampling probability", 
+ xlab = "age at diagnosis (years)")

And finally, the empirical CIFs under H1:

> plot(X[order(X)]/365, cumsum(w01), type = "s", 
+ ylab = "cumulative incidence", 
+ xlab = "age at diagnosis (years)", ylim = c(0,.37))

5.5.3 Code for Example 5.2.6

The effect of gender can be also explored through a proportional cause‐specific hazards model (just for group ICCGroup 2, the only one with significant results).

> Ch<-ChildCancer[!is.na(ChildCancer$ICCGroup),] 
> attach(Ch) 
> fz.gender <- factor(Sex, levels = 1:2) 
> levels(fz.gender) <- c("Female","Male") 
> W <- shen(X, U, V, boot = F)$biasf 
> library(survival) 
> summary(coxph(Surv(X, ICCGroup == 2) 
+ ˜ fz.gender + offset(-log(W)))

Cumulative incidences for lymphoma (corresponding to ICCGroup equal 2) and other cancers, conditionally on gender, can be computed as represented. Females (males) correspond to Sex equal to 1 (equal to 2).

> summary(coxph(Surv(X, ICCGroup != 2) 
+ ˜ fz.gender + offset(-log(W))))

The corresponding plots (for females and males) can be produced with the code below.

> Ch.f <- subset(Ch, subset = Sex == 1) 
> attach(Ch.f) 
> Xf <- X 
> res1 <- shen(X, U, V, boot = F) 
> w1 <- 1 / res1$biasf; w1 <- w1 / sum(w1) 
> w1.lymph <- w1 * as.numeric(ICCGroup == 2) 
> w1.other <- w1 * as.numeric(ICCGroup != 2) 
> Ch.m <- subset(Ch, subset = Sex == 2) 
> attach(Ch.m) 
> Xm <- X 
> res2 <- shen(X, U, V, boot = F) 
> w2 <- 1 / res2$biasf; w2 <- w2 / sum(w2) 
> w2.lymph <- w2 * as.numeric(ICCGroup==2) 
> w2.other <- w2 * as.numeric(ICCGroup!=2) 
> plot(Xf, cumsum(w1.lymph), type = "s", 
+ col = 2, ylab = "cumulative incidence", 
+ xlab = "age at diagnosis (days)", ylim = c(0,1)) 
> lines(Xf, cumsum(w1.other), type = "s", 
+  col = 2, lty = 2) 
> lines(Xm, cumsum(w2.lymph), type = "s") 
> lines(Xm, cumsum(w2.other), type = "s", lty = 2)

5.5.4 Code for Example 5.3.1

As it is indicated in Example 5.3.1, it is easy to assess quasi‐independence between the target and the truncation variables.

> library(DTDA) 
> attach(AIDS.DT) 
> library(SurvTrunc) 
> t <- indeptestDT(X, U, V)

5.5.5 Code for Example 5.4.3

To compute the nonparametric estimator of a distribution function under dependence, we consider the algorithm described in Section 5.4. This algorithm makes use of the first order derivatives of FGM, Clayton and Frank copulas, which are available in package VineCopula.

For using these specific copula models, some initial solutions ( and in step SA1 in the algorithm) must be passed. We used (being the sample size) for both variables. Then, the log likelihood of is computed using the initial solutions. The log likelihood can be maximized using optim until convergence is reached. For that purpose, a maximum error must be fixed for , and .

As an example, the log likelihood for the Clayton copula can be computed as follows:

> LIK<-function(theta){ 
+  Numlik0 <- t(log(BiCopPDF(u1 = (n/(n+1))*F0, 
+ u2 = (n/(n+1))*K0,3, theta, par2 = 0)) 
+ + log(as.vector(f)) + log(as.vector(k))) 
+  d <-as.matrix( expand.grid((n/(n+1))*F0, 
+ (n/(n+1))*K0, theta)) 
+  dCall <- BiCopPDF(d[,1], d[,2], 3, theta, par2=0) 
+  d_value <- dCall 
+  myfunc3 <- function(u, v){u*v} 
+  myfunc4 <- function(x){ 
+  u <- x[1] 
+  v <- x[2] 
+  myfunc3(u, v) 
+  } 
+  d1 <- expand.grid(f, k, theta) 
+  d1Call <- myfunCall(f, k, theta, 2) 
+  d1_value <- d1Call[,4] 
+  JIV <- rep(as.vector(J), times = length(theta)) 
+  Denomlik0 <- d_value*d1_value*JIV 
+  Denomlik1 <- matrix(data = Denomlik0, 
+ nrow = length(K0)*length(F0), ncol = length(theta)) 
+  Denomlik <- apply(Denomlik1, 2, "sum") 
+  lik0 <- apply((Numlik0-log(Denomlik)), 1, "sum") 
+  return(-lik0)}

For other copulas, when using the R function BiCopPDF of VineCopula package, we shall change the number corresponding to the desired copula family.

A
Packages and Functions in R

Throughout this book, we have mainly used the functions in package DTDA for data analyses. Nevertheless, there are also other packages in R ( R Core Team, 2020) that can be useful for analysing doubly truncated data; some of them have been already mentioned in the book chapters. In this Appendix we will briefly revised the functions included in packages DTDA.ni (de Uña‐Álvarez and Soage, 2018), DTDA.cif (de Uña‐Álvarez and Soage, 2020), SurvTrunc (Rennert, 2018) and double.truncation (Emura et al., 2019), together with the functions belonging to DTDA that have been used in the illustrative examples in this book. See Moreira et al. (2010) for an introduction to DTDA, and Moreira et al. (2021) for the description of the new functions included in its latest version 3.0.

DTDA includes a variety of functions that allow to compute the NPMLE from doubly truncated data with different algorithms, jointly with bootstrap confidence intervals, and to obtain kernel estimates of the density and hazard functions, with suitable bandwidth selectors in this setting. An alternative estimator of the NPMLE, avoiding an iterative procedure, is implemented in DTDA.ni ; see de Uña‐Álvarez (2018) for details on this non‐iterative estimator. Package double.truncation includes a function for obtaining the NPMLE jointly with an asymptotic standard error (Emura et al., 2015). Likelihood‐based methods implemented in double.truncation also enable the computation of parametric estimators. SurvTrunc also allows to get the NPMLE with bootstrap standard errors. In addition, Cox regression, as proposed by Rennert and Xie (2018), is also possible with SurvTrunc. Finally, cumulative incidence function estimation for competing risks can be done with DTDA.cif, providing the two different estimators proposed in de Uña‐Álvarez (2020a). Bootstrap standard errors for the cumulative incidences are also available from DTDA.cif.

In what follows, functions and packages (denoted as function ( package)) will be briefly described, organized according to the most relevant tasks when proceeding with a doubly truncated data analysis. In de Uña‐Álvarez (2020b) comparative studies for several of these functions can be found.

A.1 Computing the NPMLE and Standard Errors

efron.petrosian ( DTDA): the NPMLE estimator is computed using the first algorithm by Efron and Petrosian. Pointwise confidence limits can be also computed, using a simple bootstrap method.

> efron.petrosian(X, U = NA, V = NA, wt = NA, error = NA, 
+  nmaxit = NA, boot = TRUE, B = NA, alpha = NA, 
+  display.F = FALSE, display.S = FALSE)

lynden ( DTDA): the NPMLE estimator is computed using the second algorithm by Efron and Petrosian. As for the previous function, simple bootstrap (pointwise) confidence bands can be also obtained.

> lynden(X, U = NA, V = NA, error = NA, nmaxit = NA, 
+  boot = TRUE, B = NA, alpha = NA, 
+ display.F = FALSE, display.S = FALSE)

shen ( DTDA): the NPMLE estimator is computed using Shen's algorithm, jointly with marginal distributions of the truncation variables. Bootstrap (with simple or obvious methods) can be also computed.

> shen(X, U = NA, V = NA, wt = NA, error = NA, 
+  nmaxit = NA, boot = TRUE, boot.type = "simple", 
+  B = NA, alpha = NA, display.FS = FALSE, 
+ display.UV = FALSE, plot.joint = FALSE, 
+ plot.type = NULL)

DTDAni ( DTDA.ni): this function produces a non‐iterative estimator of the cumulative distribution of a doubly truncated variable, for an interval sampling scenario with interval width tau. Confidence bands are not provided.

> DTDAni(x, u, tau)

NPMLE ( double.truncation): the NPMLE is computed with Shen's algorithm and standard errors are obtained using the asymptotic variance formula in Emura et al. (2015).

> NPMLE(u.trunc, y.trunc, v.trunc,epsilon=1e-08)

cdfDT ( SurvTrunc): also using Shen's algorithm, this function provides 95% confidence limits using simple bootstrap and the normal approximation method.

> cdfDT(y, l, r, error = 1e-06, n.iter = 10000, 
+ boot = F , B.boot = 200, joint = FALSE, 
+ plot.cdf = FALSE, plot.joint = FALSE, display = TRUE)

A.2 Assessing the Existence and Uniqueness of the NPMLE

A necessary condition for the existence and uniqueness of the NPMLE can be checked as follows:

> n <- length(x) 
> c1 <- c2 <- rep(0, n) 
> for (i in 1:n){ 
+ c1[i] <- sum(as.numeric(u<= x[i] & x[i] <= v)) 
+ c2[i] <- sum(as.numeric(u[i]<=x & x<=v[i]))} 
> min(c1);min(c2)

Both min(c1) and min(c2) must be strictly greater than 1, otherwise the NPMLE does not exist or is not unique. The functions in DTDA report a warning message when min(c1)==1 or min(c2)==1.

As mentioned by Xiao and Hudgens (2019), the package igraph can be used to determine subsamples for which the NPMLE exists and is unique. Actually, such subsamples are strongly connected subgraphs as defined in Xiao and Hudgens (2019). The following lines allow to get, describe and visualize the strongly connected subgraphs from a given doubly truncated dataset with target variable x and truncation limits u and v :

> library(igraph) 
> au <- outer(x, u, ">=") 
> av <- outer(x, v, "<=") 
> J <- au * av 
> plot(graph.adjacency(J)) 
> G <- graph.adjacency(J) 
> SCC <- clusters(G, mode = "strong") 
> table(SCC$membership) 
> SCC$csize; SCC$no

A.3 Semiparametric and Parametric Estimation

PMLE.dist ( double.truncation): a series of functions performing parametric estimation. Distribution models ( dist) considered are the loglogistic, log‐normal, Weibull and special exponential families. Estimation is performed by maximum likelihood. In practice, we have found that a log‐transformation of the random variables (both target and truncation variables) is required.

Regarding the semiparametric estimation it should be noted that, although there is not a specific function in R, there are many functions that allow for including weights. For that purpose, it is useful to keep in a vector the parametric estimation of the biasing function , evaluated in the sample values. Normalized weights computed from this vector may be passed to weighted.mean or lm, among others. As a note of caution, computation of standard errors directly obtained from these functions may not be correct, since they do not incorporate the randomness of the weights.

A.4 Kernel Estimation

densityDT ( DTDA): this function computes the kernel density estimator under double truncation. Argument bw allows for choosing different bandwidth selectors, specifically: normal‐reference rule ( NR), plug‐in in one or two stages ( DPI1, DPI2), least‐squares cross‐validation ( LSCV) or smoothed bootstrap ( SBoot).

> densityDT(X, U, V, bw = "DPI2", from, to, n, wg = NA)

hazardDT ( DTDA): this function computes the kernel estimator of the hazard function under double truncation, with a LSCV bandwidth.

> hazardDT(X, U, V, bw = "LSCV", from, to, n, wg = NA)

A.5 Regression Analysis

coxDT ( SurvTrunc): this function allows to fit a Cox proportional hazards regression model, with doubly truncated survival time. It also computes bootstrap standard errors and confidence intervals. It implements the approach in Rennert and Xie (2018).

> coxDT(formula, L, R, data, subset, time.var = FALSE, 
+ subject = NULL,  B.SE.np = 200, CI.boot = F , 
+ B.CI.boot = 2000, pvalue.boot = F , 
+ B.pvalue.boot = 500, B.pvalue.se.boot = 100, 
+ trunc.weight = 100,  print.weights = FALSE, 
+ error = 10∧-6, n.iter = 1000)

Cox regression as proposed by Mandel et al. (2018) can be performed from the function coxph in package survival by introducing as an offset, where contains the evaluations of or on the sample values. In this case, the standard errors given by coxph are not valid and must be re‐calculated by bootstrapping.

A.6 Competing Risks

DTDAcif ( DTDA.cif): this function estimates nonparametrically the cumulative incidences of competing risks under double truncation.

> DTDAcif(x, u, v, comp.event, method = c("indep", "dep"), 
+  boot = F, B = 300, N.iter = 100, error = 1e-06)

Cause‐specific hazards regression can be performed from the coxph function by using as an offset the weights in the previous section.

A.7 Simulating Data

rsim.DT ( DTDA): random generation of doubly truncated data with two different patterns of observational bias, specified by arguments model and tau (the width of the sampling interval). The two implemented models correspond to the simulation scenarios I and II in Section 2.1.3.

> rsim.DT(n, tau, model = NULL)

simu.Weibull ( double.truncation): random generation of doubly truncated data from a Weibull model. Arguments mu and sigma correspond to the Weibull parameters and delta controls the inclusion probability.

> simu.Weibull(n, mu, sigma, delta)

A.8 Testing Quasi‐independence

indeptestDT ( SurvTrunc): this function computes a quasi‐independence tests based on the conditional Kendall's Tau.

> indeptestDT(x, u, v)

A.9 Dependent Truncation

BiCopPDF ( VineCopula): this function evaluates the pdf of a given bivariate copula. Argument family (a number) allows to consider the Clayton and FGM copulas, among others.

> BiCopPDF(u1, u2, family,...)
